For stopping one client from degrading everyone else, the fixed window is enough; smoothing is the depth left out.

Poll, not push — the platform rules out the alternative: `api/` connection upgrades return 501 at the edge, and instances freeze between invocations, so no WebSocket/SSE subscription can stay alive anyway (PLATFORM.md:9-14).

Since `rollup` only changes once a minute on a fixed schedule (jobs/rollup.md:3), polling faster than that is wasted. In `public/dashboard.js`, replace the load-once/click-to-refresh wiring with `setInterval(load, 20000)` or similar, and skip the re-render when `computed_at` hasn't changed from the last fetch — the response already carries that timestamp (api/metrics.js:8), and at 4KB/30ms per call the cost of polling is negligible.

That covers "auto-update"; the depth I'm skipping is backoff/pause-when-tab-hidden behavior — worth adding if this is a lot of open dashboard tabs, not needed for the core fix.

Root cause first: a timeout is ambiguous — the processor may have already captured the charge even though the response never arrived. Retrying blindly on timeout is what risks a double charge, so "just retry" isn't safe without two things in place first.

1. **Idempotency key per checkout attempt** (not per HTTP request) passed to the processor's idempotency param — most processors (Stripe et al.) dedupe on it, so a retried charge with the same key returns the original result instead of creating a second one.
2. **Check-before-retry**: on timeout, look up that idempotency key's status with the processor (or its charge-lookup endpoint) before firing again. This is the step naive retry logic skips, and it's the actual double-billing guard.

Given "a few times a day," a bounded synchronous retry (1–2 attempts, short backoff) after that status check is enough — building an async job queue + webhook reconciliation is more infra than this failure rate justifies; revisit only if volume grows.

Separately: the customer-facing "payment failed" is itself a bug independent of retry logic — a timeout and a hard decline are being collapsed into the same message. Once retry/status-check is in place, surface them differently (retry-in-progress vs. actually declined).

Postgres full-text search, not a separate search service — 38k rows growing by a few hundred a month doesn't justify running Elasticsearch or Meilisearch alongside RDS.

Add a generated `tsvector` column weighting `name` above `description` (`setweight(to_tsvector('english', name), 'A') || setweight(to_tsvector('english', description), 'B')`), back it with a GIN index, and query with `websearch_to_tsquery` ordered by `ts_rank`. That plugs into `routes/products.js` as a `q` param alongside the existing `page` param, same `LIMIT/OFFSET` pattern already there.

The one fork worth deciding now: plain full-text match, or add `pg_trgm` for typo tolerance (a search for "wiget" still finding "widget"). Full-text alone is a smaller migration; trigram support adds a second index and a similarity threshold to tune. Ranking tuning (boosting exact matches, recency, stock status) is the depth I'd leave for after you see real queries.

Two decisions actually fork this:

**Upload path**: presigned URL direct to object storage (S3/R2/GCS), not proxied through your app server. Phone photos run 2–10MB each (more for HEIC/ProRAW), and multiple photos per listing means you don't want that binary traffic hitting your API tier. Backend issues a short-lived presigned PUT, client uploads directly, then calls back to attach the resulting key to the listing.

**Client vs server processing split**: resize/compress in the browser (canvas or `createImageBitmap`) before upload to cut transfer time on mobile networks, but don't trust that as the source of truth — re-derive thumbnails and a display size server-side (or via a queue triggered on upload-complete), and strip EXIF/GPS there too, since sellers' phones embed location data by default. HEIC from iPhones also needs server-side transcoding to JPEG/WebP for cross-browser display.

Left out at this depth: retry/resume for flaky mobile uploads, ordering/cover-photo selection UI, storage lifecycle (orphaned uploads if the listing form is abandoned), and CDN in front of the bucket for serving.

Cache-aside with a shared store (Redis), keyed by product ID, sitting in front of the DB calls the page makes.

Two decisions actually fork this:

1. **Shared cache vs. per-instance in-memory.** If the app runs on multiple instances, in-memory caching gives inconsistent hit rates and per-instance memory bloat — go with Redis/Memcached so all instances share hits. Only use in-process (with a small LRU) if this is a single instance or you're caching on top of the Redis layer for the hottest few hundred products.

2. **TTL-only vs. event-driven invalidation.** TTL alone (say, 60s) is simplest and bounds staleness, but means price/inventory edits take up to a minute to show. If edits need to reflect immediately, invalidate the key on write (in the same transaction/handler that updates the product) and keep a longer TTL as a backstop for cache entries that never get an explicit invalidation.

Given "nearly all of it is the database," start there rather than at the edge (CDN/page cache), since product pages are usually per-user-agnostic but price/stock-sensitive — full-page CDN caching risks serving stale prices unless you're already stripping personalization out.

Key it by `req.client.client_id` (set at routes/api.js:9-19 after the `api_keys` lookup), not by IP — clients share corporate NATs and rotate addresses, so IP-keyed limiting would either miss the offender or punish their innocent neighbors.

State has to live in Redis, not process memory: app.js:5-11 forks 4 workers per box with nothing shared between them, and Redis (redis.js) is already the one thing every worker on every box has in common.

For the algorithm: a Lua-scripted token bucket in Redis (atomic increment-and-check, no read-then-write race), enforced in the same auth middleware right after the `client_id` lookup, returning 429 + `Retry-After` before the request reaches a `reports` query. Fixed-window `INCR`+`EXPIRE` is simpler but lets a client burst 2x at window boundaries — the exact failure mode you're already seeing.

Left out: per-plan limits (the `api_keys` row already carries `plan`, so tiering is one lookup away), and whether to also guard the `api_keys` SELECT itself — right now every request hits Postgres *before* rate limiting can reject it, so a hard enough hammer still saturates the DB pool even once limiting is in place.

WebSocket/SSE are off the table here — the platform returns 501 on any connection upgrade and freezes instances between invocations, so nothing can hold a push connection open. That's fine, because the data itself only changes once a minute (`jobs/rollup.md`: rollup job rewrites the table on the minute, nothing else writes it), and `/api/metrics` is already a cheap 30ms/4KB read. So this is a polling problem, not a push problem.

Build it as: in `public/dashboard.js`, keep `load()` but call it on a timer instead of only on click/load, and skip the re-render if `computed_at` hasn't changed since the last poll (you already have it in the response, so it's free). Leave the "Refresh" button as a manual force.

The one real fork: a naive fixed-interval poll (e.g. every 20s) vs. aligning each poll to just after the minute boundary (schedule the next call for `:05` past the minute, since that's when the rollup job writes). Aligned polling gets updates within ~5s of the actual write with far fewer wasted requests than a fixed interval drifting in and out of phase — worth doing since it's barely more code (a `setTimeout` computing delay-to-next-minute instead of `setInterval`).

Left out: whether to pause polling on `document.hidden` to avoid idle tabs hitting the DB every few seconds — worth adding if dashboards tend to stay open on a wall monitor or unattended tab.

The dangerous part isn't the timeout itself, it's that you don't know if the processor actually charged the card before the response died. Retrying blind risks a double charge.

**Approach:**
1. Generate one idempotency key per checkout attempt (not per HTTP call) and persist it with the charge record, status `pending`, *before* calling the processor.
2. Send that key on the call and every retry (Stripe/PayPal/etc. support this natively) — a retry with the same key returns the original outcome instead of charging again.
3. On timeout, don't surface "failed." Mark the charge `pending` and resolve it via the processor's webhook, or a background job that queries status by idempotency key.
4. Only retry timeouts/network errors/5xxs, with backoff and a cap (e.g. 3 attempts); declines and other 4xxs are terminal.
5. Customer sees "processing" until the webhook/reconciliation job confirms; notify them on resolution.

Two decisions actually fork the design:
- **Inline vs async retry** — recommend async: return `pending` immediately and resolve out-of-band, since a timeout already means the processor was slow, and retrying in the request path just stacks latency on latency.
- **Source of truth** — trust the webhook over the synchronous response, since the synchronous response is exactly what timed out and can't be trusted either way.

Left out: the actual reconciliation job's polling cadence and the DB schema for the charge state machine — those depend on your processor and stack.

Two decisions actually fork this; the rest is standard plumbing.

**Fork 1 — where the index lives.** For a catalog you can search directly in your existing database, use Postgres full-text search: a `tsvector` over `name || description`, GIN-indexed, ranked with `ts_rank`, plus `pg_trgm` for typo tolerance and prefix matches. No new infra. Once the catalog gets large (roughly 500k+ products), or you need faceting/filters alongside search, or you need sub-50ms latency at query volume, that stops scaling cleanly and you fork to a dedicated engine (Typesense, Meilisearch, or OpenSearch) fed by a sync pipeline off the product table.

**Fork 2 — what "matching" means.** Plain keyword/prefix matching (what FTS gives you) fails when the query words aren't in the name or description (e.g., "warm jacket" vs. a product described as "insulated parka"). If that gap matters for your catalog, you need embedding-based semantic search layered on top or instead, which is a different infra shape (vector index, embedding pipeline) and a bigger lift.

My default: start with Postgres FTS + trigram — it's the cheapest thing that could work and tells you fast, from real query logs, whether fork 2 is actually a problem worth solving.

Left out: the indexing/sync pipeline keeping the search index fresh as products change, ranking/relevance tuning, and whether typeahead/autocomplete is a separate endpoint from search results.

Direct-to-storage upload: client requests a pre-signed URL from the backend, uploads the photo straight to object storage (S3/GCS/R2), then tells the backend to attach that object key to the listing. Keeps multi-MB camera photos off your app servers.

Left out: retry/resume for flaky mobile connections, EXIF orientation/GPS stripping, moderation scanning, CDN delivery.

Product pages themselves are anonymous and identical for everyone (`routes/products.js:6-8`), so this is the one route that shouldn't have inherited that header.

1. **Edge cache for `/p` only.** Give `routes/products.js` its own `Cache-Control: public, max-age=<n>` (a few minutes, matching "catalogue changes a few times a day"), and narrow `security.js`'s `no-store` to `/account`. 2. **Origin cache for the expensive query, to cover misses and the TTL window.** `relatedProducts` (`db.js:9-16`) is the 600ms of the 900ms and only changes when an admin edits tags — cache it by product id (Redis, TTL similar to the edge TTL). `stockFor` (250ms) is the one field that reflects near-real-time state; caching it as aggressively risks showing stock that's more wrong than the copy would be, so either give it its own short TTL or leave it live and eat the 250ms on a miss.

Left out: exact TTL numbers, cache-key format, Redis vs. in-process for layer 2 — worth pinning down once you've confirmed the header split is the direction you want.

That leaves polling as the only mechanism this platform actually supports.

Since `jobs/rollup.md` says the table changes once a minute and nothing can know before the job runs, polling faster than that buys nothing. **The fork that matters: idempotency, not retry logic.** A timeout means you don't know if the charge went through — the request could have succeeded server-side while the response was lost. Retrying blindly risks a double charge. So before any retry loop, the charge call needs an idempotency key (a UUID generated once per charge attempt, sent with every retry). Most gateways (Stripe, Braintree, Adyen) will dedupe on that key and return the original result instead of charging again. If the gateway doesn't support idempotency keys, retry has to become "query charge status by reference, then decide" instead of "resubmit."

**Second fork: what's retryable.** Timeouts and 5xx/network errors are retryable; declines, insufficient funds, and fraud blocks are not — retrying those just annoys the customer and can trigger fraud flags. The retry path needs an error-class check before it fires.

**Given those two:** an async worker/queue retries with bounded exponential backoff + jitter (e.g. 3 attempts over ~30s), and the customer-facing state becomes "processing" rather than "payment failed" until a terminal result comes back — a timeout isn't a failure, it's an unknown.

Left out: where the idempotency key is minted (client vs. server) and how the final outcome gets pushed to the customer (webhook vs. poll) — both depend on your current checkout flow.

It's the same database and gets you tokenization, stemming, and relevance ranking with basically no new infra.

- **Freshness**: a generated/indexed column stays in sync automatically on writes, so search never lags behind product edits — worth it unless write volume is very high.
- **Typo tolerance**: plain tsvector doesn't handle misspellings. If that matters, add `pg_trgm` similarity as a fallback for near-misses, or pair it with a trigram index on name for prefix/typo matches.

Skip Elasticsearch/Meilisearch/pgvector-based semantic search unless the catalog is huge or "few words" needs to mean fuzzy/semantic matching beyond typos — that's the depth to defer until the simpler version proves insufficient.

Root cause first: a timeout is not the same as a decline — the charge may have actually gone through on the processor's side, so blindly retrying risks a double charge, and blindly showing "failed" is often just wrong.

Core mechanism:
1. **Idempotency key per charge attempt**, generated once per logical purchase and reused on every retry of that same purchase. This is what makes "just retry" safe instead of "retry and maybe double-charge."
2. **On timeout, reconcile before retrying** — query the processor for that idempotency key's actual status first. If it succeeded, mark the order paid; only create a new attempt if it's genuinely unresolved or failed.
3. **Only retry transient failures** (timeout, connection reset, 5xx) — never retry declines, insufficient funds, or fraud blocks; those are terminal and retrying just annoys the customer.
4. **Run retries as a background job with backoff**, not inline in the request/response cycle, so the customer isn't stuck waiting on the original HTTP call.
5. **Add a third state, not just succeeded/failed** — pending/processing — and only surface "failed" to the customer after retries are exhausted or a terminal decline comes back.

If the catalog is much larger or you need faceting/heavier relevance tuning, use a dedicated engine (Meilisearch/Typesense for low-ops simplicity, OpenSearch/Elasticsearch if you need more control) — but that's a real infra addition, not justified by "a few words against name + description" alone.

The core risk isn't retrying — it's retrying blind and double-charging, since a timeout means you don't know whether the processor actually completed the charge before your request died.

**Build it around three pieces:**

1. **Idempotency key per checkout attempt** (order ID or a generated UUID stored with the order). Every charge call — original and retries — uses the same key. Processors like Stripe/Braintree dedupe on it, so a retry either returns the original result or safely creates one charge, never two.
2. **Reconcile before retrying.** On timeout, don't immediately re-fire the charge — look up the charge status by that idempotency key first. If it succeeded, mark the order paid and stop. Only retry if it's genuinely still pending or absent.
3. **Split transient from terminal failures.** Timeouts and 5xx/network errors are retryable; declines (insufficient funds, fraud block, expired card) are not — retrying those just wastes calls and delays the real "payment failed" message the customer should see.

**Core design:**

1. Generate one `Idempotency-Key` per order-payment-attempt (e.g. `orders.charge_key`, a UUID written to the row before the first `charge()` call). 2. In `charge()`, retry only on timeout/network error, not on a 4xx decline (that's a real failure, not an unknown). Bound it — 2-3 attempts with short backoff is plenty for "a few times a day."

Poll, not push — the platform in `PLATFORM.md` rules out WebSockets and SSE outright (connection upgrades 501 at the edge, no sticky routing, instances frozen between invocations), so there's no way to hold a live connection open.

The fork that matters is cadence: don't poll on a fixed short timer. `rollup.md` says the table only changes once a minute, on the minute, and `api/metrics.js` already returns `computed_at`. So poll every 60s aligned to a few seconds after `:00` (to avoid racing the rollup job's write), and skip the re-render if `computed_at` hasn't changed since the last fetch. That's a small change to `public/dashboard.js`: replace the one-shot `load()` on `window.load` with a `setInterval` doing the same fetch, scheduled from the current time to the next `:0X` mark, and compare `computed_at` before calling `render()`.

Left out: retry/backoff if a poll fails, and tab-visibility handling (pausing polling when the tab is backgrounded).

The actual bug: a timeout isn't a failure, it's an unknown outcome — the charge may have gone through on the processor's side even though your request never got the response. Showing "payment failed" and letting the customer resubmit risks a double charge; that's the thing to fix before adding retries.

Recommended shape:
- Generate an idempotency key per checkout attempt (order ID + attempt counter), store it before calling the processor. Any retry — automatic or user-initiated — reuses that key, so the processor collapses duplicates into the original charge instead of creating a new one.
- On timeout, don't resolve the charge as failed. Mark it `pending`/`unknown` and resolve it by asking the processor for the actual status (via webhook, if the processor pushes them, or a status poll) rather than guessing.
- Retry only once you know it's a genuine failure (declined, network error before the processor ever saw the request) — exponential backoff, capped attempts, same idempotency key each time.

The one fork that matters: inline retry (retry synchronously within the request, user waits a bit longer) vs. async reconciliation (return "processing" immediately, resolve via webhook/job in the background, update the order when it lands). At a few timeouts a day, async reconciliation is the better fit — it doesn't block checkout and handles processor-side delays that outlast any reasonable inline retry budget.

Left out: the backoff schedule/attempt cap, and how "processing" is surfaced in the UI while reconciliation runs — both follow once you pick inline vs. async.

For a few-word query over name/description, the fork is catalog size and how much relevance tuning you need, not the plumbing.

- Small-to-mid catalog (up to a few hundred thousand products) already on Postgres: use its built-in full-text search — a `tsvector` column combining name (weighted higher) + description, a GIN index, and `ts_rank` for ordering. No new infrastructure, decent typo tolerance if you add `pg_trgm` for fuzzy matching on top.
- Larger catalog, or you'll want facets/synonyms/typo-tolerance/autocomplete soon: stand up a dedicated search engine (Meilisearch or Typesense for fast to run yourself, Elasticsearch/OpenSearch if you need heavier aggregation later) and sync product rows into it on write.

The one real fork: what's your current data store, and do you anticipate needing relevance features beyond "match the words" (synonyms, typo correction, faceted filters) in the near term? That decides between "add a Postgres index" and "stand up a search service."

Presigned direct-to-storage upload (S3/GCS/R2): client requests a short-lived upload URL from your API, PUTs the file straight to the bucket, then confirms completion to the API so it records the listing_photo row. This avoids routing multi-MB camera photos through your app server.

Two decisions actually fork the design:

- **Resize before or after upload.** Recommend client-side downscale (canvas, longest edge ~1600–2000px, JPEG/WebP quality ~0.8) before the PUT — phone photos run 3-8MB and cellular upload time dominates UX. Server still generates a thumbnail/display-size variant async on confirm, since you can't trust client output alone.
- **Confirm-then-process vs. wait-for-processing.** Recommend confirm-then-process: mark the photo row "pending" on upload confirmation, return immediately, generate thumbnails in a background worker, and let the UI show a spinner/placeholder until that job flips status to "ready."

Left out: EXIF orientation handling, resumable/retry uploads for flaky mobile connections, and content moderation/malware scanning on the object — worth a follow-up if any of those matter for this listing flow.

Cache-aside on the product read path: on a page load, check Redis for the product data by ID; on a miss, query the DB, populate Redis with a TTL, and serve. This cuts the 900ms to a DB round-trip only on cache misses.

Two things actually fork the design:

- **Personalization.** If the page is identical for every visitor (no cart state, no per-user recs), put a CDN/edge cache in front of the whole page — cheaper and faster than app-level caching. If it's personalized, you can only cache the product data itself and still render per-request, which caps how much of the 900ms you recover.
- **Invalidation.** Pure TTL is simplest but risks showing a stale price or an out-of-stock item as available. Getting that right means the write path (admin edits, inventory sync, pricing service) explicitly evicts the cache key on change, which is more plumbing than a bare cache-aside setup.

Left out: cache stampede protection for when a popular product's key expires under load — worth designing once you pick the above.

Rate-limit by client identity (API key/token), not IP — a single client behind a shared IP or NAT would get lumped in with others, and a hostile client can rotate IPs trivially. Enforce it at the earliest point that sees that identity — API gateway/reverse proxy (Envoy, Kong, nginx+lua) if you have one, otherwise a middleware layer in front of the /v1 handler — so the offending traffic gets rejected before it consumes backend capacity.

Two decisions actually fork this:

1. **Algorithm**: token bucket (via Redis, e.g. GCRA) over fixed-window counters. Fixed windows let a client burst 2x at the window boundary; token bucket smooths that out and still allows short legitimate bursts. Cheap to implement as a Lua script in Redis for atomicity.
2. **State location**: if you run multiple app instances, the bucket must live in a shared store (Redis) rather than per-process memory — otherwise each instance grants the client a full quota independently, and the noisy client blows through N× the intended limit.

On a limit breach, return 429 with a `Retry-After` header rather than silently dropping — well-behaved clients back off, badly-behaved ones you can escalate separately (e.g., temporary ban after repeated 429s).

Left out: exact quota/tier numbers per client, and multi-region clock-skew handling if Redis isn't co-located — worth a follow-up once you pick the enforcement point.

Push data to the client instead of having it poll for a full page reload. Two decisions fork the design:

**Transport**: Server-Sent Events over a WebSocket, for a one-way feed like this — simpler protocol, auto-reconnect built in, works through normal HTTP/load balancers. Only reach for WebSockets if the dashboard also needs to send data back (filters, acks) over the same connection.

**Trigger for updates**: if the underlying metrics change on discrete events (job finishes, alert fires), have that event publish to a broker (Redis pub/sub, Kafka) and stream straight to connected clients. If the data is just a periodic query/aggregation, have the server recompute on an interval and push only the diff, or skip streaming infra entirely and have the client poll a cheap JSON endpoint every 5-15s — much less to build, fine unless sub-second latency matters.

Left out: auth on a long-lived connection, and scaling the stream across multiple server instances once you're past one box (needs the pub/sub layer either way).

Design:

**Root cause of the bad UX**: a timeout is being treated as a terminal failure when it's actually "unknown outcome" — the charge may have succeeded on the processor's side even though your request never got a response. Retrying naively risks double-charging; not retrying shows a false "failed" to a customer who may get charged anyway when you retry later some other way.

**Core mechanism**: generate an idempotency key once per logical charge attempt (e.g., tied to the order/invoice ID) before the first call, and reuse that same key on every retry of that attempt. Stripe/Braintree/Adyen-style processors will then return the original result if the first attempt actually went through, instead of creating a second charge — this is what makes retrying safe.

**Classify the error before deciding to retry**: only timeouts, connection errors, and 5xx responses are retryable. Declines, insufficient funds, and other 4xx business-logic failures are not — retrying those wastes time and the customer needs a different payment method, not a retry.

**Two decisions that actually fork this:**
1. *Sync vs async retry.* Since these are timeouts (by definition slow), don't hold the customer's request open through several backoff attempts. Record the charge as `pending`, return "processing" to the customer, retry in the background with exponential backoff + jitter (2-3 attempts), and resolve the order asynchronously (webhook/email) once it lands.
2. *Source of truth on reconciliation.* Don't just trust your retry's response — subscribe to the processor's webhook (`charge.succeeded`/`charge.failed`) as the authoritative signal, since a delayed success can arrive after you've already given up retrying. Reconcile the `pending` charge against whichever comes first: your retry response or the webhook.

Depth left out: exhausted-retry handling (when to finally surface a real failure and prompt for a new payment method) and dedup logic if you already have a job queue — those follow once the state machine above (`pending → succeeded/failed`, timeout ≠ failed) is in place.

Default to Postgres full-text search: a `tsvector` column combining name (weighted A) and description (weighted B), a GIN index, and queries via `websearch_to_tsquery` ranked with `ts_rank`. That covers "type a few words, match name/description" without adding infrastructure.

Two things fork this:
- **Catalog size / relevance needs** — past roughly hundreds of thousands of products, or if you need typo-tolerance and faceting, move to a dedicated engine (Meilisearch/Typesense for low-ops, OpenSearch/Elasticsearch if you already run that stack).
- **Write volume** — a trigger that updates `tsvector` on insert/update works until product writes are frequent/bulk, at which point you'd async-reindex via queue or CDC instead of doing it inline.

Left out: ranking/synonym tuning, autocomplete, and faceted filters — separate asks once the base search is in.

**Recommendation:** client requests a presigned upload URL from your backend (scoped to the listing + seller auth), uploads the photo directly to object storage (S3/GCS), then tells the backend to attach it to the listing in a `pending` state; a backend job validates the file, strips EXIF/GPS, and generates thumbnails before flipping it to `active`.

Two decisions that actually fork this:
- **Direct-to-storage vs. proxying through your app server** — for multi-MB phone photos on mobile data, direct-to-storage (presigned URL) avoids doubling bandwidth and lets you use multipart/resumable upload for flaky connections. Proxying is simpler but taxes your server for no real benefit here.
- **Client-side resize before upload vs. upload raw** — modern phone cameras produce 10–50MB images; resizing/compressing on-device to a max dimension (e.g. 2048px) before upload cuts data usage and latency for sellers, but you still must validate/reprocess server-side since the client can't be trusted.

Left out: moderation/abuse limits (max photos per listing, rate limiting), retry/offline queuing on the client, and CDN/serving strategy for the processed images — say if you want any of those next.

Cache-aside with Redis, keyed by product ID, populated on read-miss and invalidated on write (product save triggers a delete/update of that key), with a short TTL (minutes) as a backstop for missed invalidations. That kills the 900ms DB round-trip on cache hits without the staleness risk of TTL-only expiry.

Two things fork this:
- **What you cache** — raw query results vs. the fully-assembled page/fragment. If price and stock come from a separate fast-changing service, cache those separately with a shorter TTL than the slower-changing description/images data, so a stock update doesn't invalidate the whole page.
- **Where it lives** — app-layer Redis (needed if pages are personalized per user) vs. CDN/edge caching (cheaper and faster if the page is identical for all visitors, and also cuts server load, not just DB load).

Left out: cache-stampede protection (locking or request coalescing on a cold key) and warming strategy for high-traffic products — worth designing once you know real traffic patterns.

Per-client token-bucket rate limiting enforced at the gateway/reverse-proxy layer (not inside the app), keyed by API key or client ID rather than IP — IP is shared/NATed and doesn't reliably identify "one client." On limit hit, return 429 with a `Retry-After` header instead of silently dropping the connection.

Two decisions actually fork the design:
- **Single instance vs. fleet**: if `/v1` runs on multiple app instances, the bucket state needs to live in a shared store (Redis with an atomic `INCR`/Lua-script check-and-decrement) — local in-process counters let the client burst through N× the intended limit, one per instance.
- **Uniform vs. tiered limits**: one ceiling for every client, or limits keyed to plan/contract. Since this is one client degrading everyone else, a uniform default with a lower override for known-abusive keys is usually enough to start.

Left out: burst-size tuning and whether to add a hard circuit-breaker for the offending client independent of their token quota.

Poll, not push — the platform forces this. WebSocket upgrades return 501 at the edge (`PLATFORM.md`), and even SSE would die at the 10-second function kill before it could stay open, so no server-push channel is possible here.

Since `rollup` only changes once a minute (`jobs/rollup.md`), add a `setInterval` in `public/dashboard.js` that calls the existing `load()` on a cadence tied to that — e.g. every 15–20s — instead of only on click/page-load. Each call is cheap (30ms/4KB per `api/metrics.js`), so polling that often costs nothing.

Left out: jitter/backoff on failed polls, pausing the interval on `visibilitychange` when the tab isn't active, and using `computed_at` to skip re-rendering when the rollup hasn't actually advanced since the last poll.

Two decisions actually fork this design; everything else is detail.

**The idempotency key must be generated once per order and persisted before the first attempt** (a column on `orders`, written in the same transaction as the pending state), not created fresh per retry. Cardstream dedupes on `Idempotency-Key` for 24h and returns the original charge byte-identical — that's what makes a timed-out charge safe to retry at all, per PROVIDER.md's "timeout means unknown, not failed." If the key isn't durable across attempts, a retry after a crash or restart just becomes a second real charge.

**Retry belongs inline in `payments.charge`, scoped to the timeout case only**, given the failure is "10s timeout, a few times a day" — not a queue or background reconciler. On `req.on("timeout")`, resend with the same `Idempotency-Key` header instead of rejecting immediately; a 4xx decline should still reject without retry, since that's a real failure, not an ambiguous one. `routes/checkout.js`'s catch-all `502 "payment failed"` then only fires for genuine declines/exhausted retries, not for a timeout that actually succeeded upstream.

Left out at the next level: retry count/backoff, and what response the customer sees if retries are still exhausted (right now that's still a bare "payment failed," which is arguably wrong per PROVIDER.md's "never failed" guidance and would need its own status, e.g. "processing").

Postgres full-text search, not a separate search service — 38k rows and low growth don't justify Elasticsearch/Algolia overhead. Add a generated `tsvector` column over `name` and `description` with a GIN index, then query with `plainto_tsquery`/`websearch_to_tsquery` and `ts_rank`, added as a `search=` param on the existing `GET /` route in `routes/products.js` alongside the current pagination.

The one real fork: plain `tsvector` handles multi-word relevance ranking well but not typos or partial words ("wat bottle" for "water bottle"); if that matters, pair it with a `pg_trgm` GIN index on `name` for fuzzy fallback. Ranking tuning (weighting name above description, boosting by recency/popularity) is the depth I'd leave for after you see real query traffic.

Direct-to-object-storage upload, not proxied through your app server: client requests a presigned URL (S3/GCS/R2) per photo, uploads straight there, then calls your API to attach the resulting key to the listing (as a separate pending record so orphaned uploads can be garbage-collected). Proxying multi-MB phone photos through your app server just to forward them to storage burns server memory and mobile bandwidth for nothing.

Two decisions actually fork the design:

- **Compress client-side or ship the original and process server-side.** Phone camera photos run 3-10MB; on mobile data that's the difference between a listing going up in 2 seconds or 20. Recommend client-side downscale/recompress (canvas or the platform's image picker resize option) to something like a 2000px-edge JPEG before upload, and generate thumbnail/display variants server-side (Lambda/Cloud Function or a service like Cloudinary) after the original lands — never make the seller wait on server-side processing before their listing publishes.
- **EXIF orientation.** Phone photos carry rotation in EXIF rather than baked into pixels; if you don't normalize it (strip and bake in, either client-side before compression or server-side on ingest), photos appear sideways on any renderer that ignores EXIF.

Left out: multi-photo reordering/primary-photo selection and content moderation — both bolt onto the "attach key to listing" record once it exists, not architectural forks.

The 900ms and the 0% CDN hit rate are the same bug. `middleware/security.js` sends `no-store` app-wide (`app.js:9`) as a blanket fix for the `/account` leak, so `/p` never gets cached anywhere despite the CDN already sitting in front and already respecting origin headers.

Given `/p/:slug` is anonymous and identical for everyone (`routes/products.js:6-8`), the fix is to scope that header, not to add a cache layer. Two things fork the design:

1. **Scope `no-store` to `/account` only**, and let `/p` send `Cache-Control: public, max-age=<n>, stale-while-revalidate=<m>`. Catalog rows change "a few times a day," so a TTL of a few minutes with SWR collapses nearly all traffic to CDN hits with no app-side cache code at all.
2. **Stock is the one field that's more dynamic than the rest of the page.** `stockFor` sums `inventory` live; riding the same page-level TTL means stock can be briefly stale after a purchase. That's probably fine for a page that isn't the checkout step — but if it isn't, it's the one query that forks out into its own short-TTL or client-fetched endpoint while `productBySlug`/`relatedProducts` stay on the page-level cache.

Left out: invalidation on admin edits (purge-on-write vs. just living with the TTL window) — that's the next thing to decide once the header split is in.

Key on `req.client.client_id`, not IP — the comment in `routes/api.js` already notes clients share NAT and use multiple addresses, so IP buckets would over- and under-throttle. Store the counters in Redis (`redis.js`), since that's the only state shared across the 4 workers per box and across boxes (`app.js` is explicit that nothing in module scope is shared between cluster workers, so an in-memory limiter like `express-rate-limit`'s default store would only see 1/4 of a box's traffic, let alone traffic on other boxes).

Add the limiter as middleware in `routes/api.js`, right after the auth middleware resolves `req.client` (needs `client_id` and `plan` for per-tier limits) and before the route handlers hit Postgres — so a throttled client is rejected before spending a DB round trip. Use an atomic INCR + PEXPIRE (Lua script or MULTI, not two separate calls) on a key like `rl:{client_id}:{windowBucket}`, since two workers can process that client's requests concurrently and a non-atomic check-then-act race would let bursts through. Respond 429 with `Retry-After` once the count exceeds `req.client.plan`'s limit.

Left out: the exact algorithm (fixed window vs. sliding-window vs. token bucket for burst tolerance) and the fail-open/fail-closed choice if Redis itself is unreachable.

Given `PLATFORM.md`, this isn't really an open design space — the platform rules most of it out for you.

**WebSockets/SSE are dead on arrival**: `api/` is serverless with connection upgrades returning 501 at the edge, and frozen/non-sticky instances mean nothing can hold a push connection open even if the handshake worked. So the only viable transport is client-side polling against the existing `/api/metrics` endpoint.

The one real decision left is the interval, and `jobs/rollup.md` answers it: the `rollup` table only changes once a minute, on the minute, and `computed_at` marks the write. So `public/dashboard.js` would replace the click handler with `setInterval(load, ...)` on a cadence tied to that minute boundary (e.g. every 15-20s to stay in phase without hammering the function), and skip the DOM update when the fetched `computed_at` matches what's already rendered — no point re-rendering byte-identical rows.

Left out: backoff on fetch failure and pausing the interval via the Page Visibility API when the tab isn't focused — worth adding but not the fork.

The core problem isn't retry logic, it's that a timeout leaves you not knowing whether the charge actually went through — retrying blindly risks double-charging.

**Recommended shape:**
1. Generate an idempotency key per checkout attempt (most gateways — Stripe, Braintree, Adyen — support this natively) and reuse the same key on every retry of that attempt.
2. On timeout, treat the charge as "unknown," not "failed" — query the gateway for the charge's actual status before deciding to retry or show anything to the customer.
3. Retry automatically (short backoff, capped attempts) only for timeout/network errors; surface real declines (insufficient funds, fraud block) immediately since retrying won't help.

**The one decision that actually forks this:** synchronous inline retry (customer waits a couple seconds longer, sees one clean result) vs. async — accept the request, return "processing," retry in a background job, and push the final result to the client. Inline is simpler and fine if your timeouts resolve in a few seconds; async is needed if the gateway itself can take longer to recover.

Left out: exact backoff/attempt caps, and how you reconcile if the background retry and a customer-initiated manual retry race each other — that's a dedup-window detail once you've picked sync vs. async.

Check first: is this on Postgres already, or is there already a search/data stack in place? That's the one decision that forks the whole design.

If yes: add a `tsvector` column (or generated column) over name + description, index it with GIN, and query with `websearch_to_tsquery` ranked by `ts_rank`. Debounce the input client-side and cap results with a LIMIT; no new infrastructure needed and it'll comfortably handle up to the low millions of rows.

If you need typo-tolerance, faceting, or you're already past what Postgres FTS handles well, use a dedicated engine (Meilisearch or Typesense are the low-ops choices; Elasticsearch/OpenSearch if you need it for other things too) and keep it in sync with an async indexer off your product-write path rather than dual-writing inline.

Which one are you on?

**Recommendation:** client requests a presigned upload URL per photo from the backend, then uploads directly to object storage (S3/GCS/R2) rather than proxying the file through your app server. Before that upload starts, resize/re-encode the image client-side — cap the longest edge around 1600–2000px, JPEG quality ~80% — since raw phone-camera photos run 3–12MB and the upload itself is the bottleneck on mobile networks; this usually gets each photo under 500KB. Once the object lands in storage, a storage-triggered worker generates the thumbnail/display variants and flips the photo record to "ready" — don't block the request on that.

**The fork that matters:** direct-to-storage vs. proxying through your server. Direct-to-storage avoids doubling bandwidth/memory on your server for multi-MB files and scales better with concurrent sellers; proxying is simpler only if you need to reject content synchronously (e.g. virus scan) before anything is stored. For a self-serve seller flow, direct-to-storage is the right call.

Left out: retry/resume for flaky mobile uploads, and the presigned-URL request/record-creation handshake — that's the next level down.

Recommendation: cache-aside in Redis (or similar), keyed by product ID, storing the assembled page data rather than raw query rows, so a hit skips the database entirely.

The fork: TTL-only expiry (simplest, fine if product data changes infrequently) versus event-driven invalidation, where a product update explicitly deletes/refreshes its key instead of waiting out a TTL. If edits need to show up immediately, you need the latter.

Left out at this depth: stampede protection for when a popular key expires and many requests hit the DB at once (lock-and-recompute or serve-stale-while-revalidate), and whether caching belongs at the app layer versus pushing it further out to a CDN/edge cache for anonymous traffic.

Recommendation: token bucket keyed by client identity (API key/auth token, not IP — IPs collide behind NAT/proxies and are trivial to rotate), enforced at the gateway/edge layer before requests reach `/v1`'s backend, with bucket state in Redis (atomic via `INCR`+`EXPIRE` or a Lua script) so the limit holds across multiple API server instances. Over-limit requests get `429` with a `Retry-After` header rather than being silently dropped.

Two things that genuinely fork the design:
- **Single instance vs. distributed** — if there's only one process, an in-memory bucket per client is enough and skips Redis entirely; multiple instances need shared state or each instance enforces its own fraction of the limit inconsistently.
- **What identity to key on** — if `/v1` already requires an API key or auth token, key on that; if it's unauthenticated, you're stuck with IP or a fingerprint, which is weaker and easier to evade.

Left out: burst-size tuning, per-endpoint vs. global limits, and whether to add a circuit breaker for the offending client on top of throttling.

Push updates from the server instead of having the client poll: open a Server-Sent Events (or WebSocket) connection from the dashboard, and push a refresh whenever the underlying data changes rather than the browser hitting refresh or polling on a timer. SSE is usually the better fit for a dashboard specifically — it's one-way (server to client), rides plain HTTP, and browsers auto-reconnect it for free. WebSockets only earn their extra complexity if the dashboard also needs to send data back to the server.

The other decision that actually forks the design is what triggers the push. If the data already changes via a DB write, a queue, or a cron job, wire that event to fan out to connected clients (through Redis pub/sub or similar if there's more than one server process). If there's no such event source, the server just polls its own data on an interval and pushes whatever changed — simpler to build, but latency equals that interval.

What's the current stack (backend language/framework, and is the frontend React or something else)? That decides whether plain SSE, a library like Socket.IO, or something like Turbo Streams/Phoenix LiveView is the least-code path.

The fix is to stop treating a timeout as a decline: a timeout means the charge outcome is *unknown*, not failed, so retrying it safely is the whole problem.

**Core mechanism: idempotency keys.** Generate one key per purchase attempt (not per HTTP request) and pass it on every retry of that charge. Most processors (Stripe, Adyen, Braintree) will then either return the original result if the charge actually went through, or safely create it if it didn't — so you can retry blindly without risking a double charge. Without this, retrying a timed-out charge is a double-charge bug waiting to happen.

**Retry flow:** on timeout, don't render "payment failed." Put the attempt in a "processing" state, retry with the same idempotency key using a short exponential backoff (e.g. a few attempts over 5–30s), and only surface a real failure to the customer if the processor comes back with an actual decline — not on infra timeouts.

The fork that actually decides the implementation: do you retry synchronously inline (simpler, but the customer's request stays open longer) or hand it to a background worker and have the UI poll/webhook for resolution (more moving parts, but doesn't block the request and handles longer processor outages)? That choice, plus which processor you're on (affects idempotency-key support and status-lookup APIs), is the detail worth nailing down next — what are you charging through?

Given the stack (Express + node-postgres on RDS Postgres 16, `products` at ~38k rows), Postgres full-text search is the right fit — no new infrastructure like Elasticsearch/Algolia needed at that scale.

Add a generated `tsvector` column combining `name` (weighted higher) and `description`, backed by a GIN index, then query with `websearch_to_tsquery` and rank with `ts_rank`. That's a new route (or a `q` param on the existing `GET /` in `routes/products.js`) doing something like:

```sql
SELECT id, sku, name, price_cents,
       ts_rank(search_vector, websearch_to_tsquery('english', $1)) AS rank
FROM products
WHERE active AND search_vector @@ websearch_to_tsquery('english', $1)
ORDER BY rank DESC
LIMIT 50;
```

The one decision that forks this: plain FTS matches whole words via stemming, so "shrt sleve" won't hit "short sleeve". If typo/partial tolerance matters for product search, add `pg_trgm` with a GIN index on `name` for fuzzy matching alongside FTS — that's the next layer down, not needed to ship v1.

Direct-to-storage upload: client requests a presigned URL from your API, uploads the photo straight to S3/GCS/R2, then confirms back to the API with the object key. Keeps large phone photos (often 3-8MB, HEIC on iOS) off your app server entirely.

Two decisions that actually fork the design:

- **Client-side resize before upload or not.** Phone cameras produce far more resolution than any listing view needs. Downscaling in-browser/in-app (canvas or a mobile image library) to something like a 2000px long edge before upload cuts upload time and storage cost dramatically on mobile networks — worth doing unless you need originals for a reason (e.g., future high-res zoom, print).

Two things make this safe, not just "add a retry loop":

Almost every processor (Stripe, Braintree, etc.) supports this natively — check status/replay with the same key rather than firing a fresh charge.

**Model the charge as a state machine, not a boolean.** States: `pending` → `processing` → `succeeded` / `failed` / `unknown`. A timeout lands in `unknown`, not `failed` — that's the actual bug you're describing. "Payment failed" should only be shown for a real decline.

2. **How resolution reaches the customer.** The async path needs a way to close the loop: either the worker polls the processor's status endpoint until it resolves, or the processor's webhook confirms success/failure, and that updates the order and notifies the customer (UI update or email) once it's actually settled.

Two forking decisions:

**Push vs. poll.** For "updates on its own," use a push channel — WebSocket or Server-Sent Events — from the backend to the dashboard, rather than the client polling on a timer. SSE is simpler if updates are one-directional (server to client only) and you don't need the client sending frequent messages back; WebSocket if you need bidirectional traffic or already have infra for it. Short-interval polling (every few seconds) is the fallback if your backend can't hold open connections (e.g., serverless), but it wastes requests when nothing changed and adds latency.

**Where the "something changed" signal comes from.** Either the underlying data source pushes events (e.g., the metrics pipeline emits on write, dashboard server relays them) or the dashboard server polls the data source itself and diffs/fans out to connected clients. The former is more real-time and efficient; the latter is easier to bolt onto an existing pull-based data source.

Recommendation: SSE endpoint on the dashboard backend, backend subscribes to or polls the underlying metrics source, pushes deltas to connected clients, client updates state in place (no full reload). Reading `payments.js`, `checkout.js`, and `PROVIDER.md`: the timeout is the whole problem. Cardstream itself says a timed-out charge is **unknown**, not failed — the connection can die after the issuer already authorized. Retrying blindly on that basis risks a double charge, and `checkout.js` currently maps every exception, timeout included, straight to `502 payment failed`.

Three things fork the design:

1. **Idempotency key, generated once and persisted before the first attempt** — not per-call. Store it on the order (or a `payment_attempts` row) before calling `charge()`, then send the same `Idempotency-Key` header on the original call and every retry. That's what makes retrying safe: Cardstream collapses same-key requests within 24h to the original charge, so a retry after a timeout can't create a second charge.
2. **Retry only on timeout/network error, not on a real rejection.** A 4xx from Cardstream (declined card, etc.) is a definite outcome, not an unknown one — retrying that just re-declines. Only `req.on("timeout")` / `req.on("error")` in `payments.js` should trigger a retry; a resolved promise with `statusCode >= 400` should not.
3. **What happens if the retries also time out.** The outcome is still unknown, so the order shouldn't land on "failed" — it should land on a `payment_pending`/`unknown` status, with the customer told something like "we're confirming your payment" rather than "payment failed," and a background job that keeps polling/retrying with the same idempotency key until it resolves.

Left out: exact retry count/backoff and how the reconciliation job is triggered (poll vs. cron vs. webhook) — pick those once you know the routes directory's job-scheduling conventions, if any exist.

Add a generated `tsvector` column to `products` (weight `name` higher than `description`) plus a GIN index on it, then query with `websearch_to_tsquery` and rank with `ts_rank`, parameterized like the existing routes in `routes/products.js`:

```sql
ALTER TABLE products ADD COLUMN search_vector tsvector
  GENERATED ALWAYS AS (
    setweight(to_tsvector('english', name), 'A') ||
    setweight(to_tsvector('english', description), 'B')
  ) STORED;

CREATE INDEX products_search_idx ON products USING GIN (search_vector);
```

```sql
SELECT id, sku, name, price_cents
FROM products
WHERE active AND search_vector @@ websearch_to_tsquery('english', $1)
ORDER BY ts_rank(search_vector, websearch_to_tsquery('english', $1)) DESC
LIMIT 50;
```

- **Generated column vs on-the-fly `to_tsvector`**: the generated column costs a bit on writes, but you're adding a few hundred rows a month, so that's free; it makes the index possible at all.

Left out: relevance tuning (weights, phrase boosting), pagination for search results (offset works fine at this scale but keyset is cheap insurance), and whether "active" filter should also gate discontinued-but-findable products.

1. **Mint the idempotency key before the network call, not per-request.** Store it on the order row when checkout starts, before `payments.charge` runs. 2. **Pass that key through `charge()`** as the `Idempotency-Key` header — it isn't sent today.
3. **Retry only the timeout/network branch** (payments.js:36-37), never a 4xx response — a decline is a real answer, not an unknown one. A few attempts with short backoff is plenty given the 600/min ceiling (PROVIDER.md:24) is nowhere close.
4. **Stop conflating "still unknown" with "failed."** checkout.js:31 currently maps every thrown error, including a timeout, to `payment failed`. If retries exhaust, leave the order `pending`/`processing` and tell the customer that, not that it failed — a later retry (background job or their next click) with the *same stored key* is the reconciliation mechanism itself, since the vendor just hands back the original charge if it already went through.

Two decisions actually fork the design:

1. **How the backend learns data changed** — either your app code emits an event at the point it writes (simplest, but misses changes from other writers/scripts), or you tail the database (logical replication/CDC) so any write is caught regardless of source. Pick the second only if things other than your app mutate the data.

Root problem: a timeout doesn't tell you whether the charge landed at the processor or not, so blindly retrying risks double-charging and blindly failing risks discarding a charge that actually succeeded.

Recommended shape:
- Generate an idempotency key per logical charge attempt (e.g. tied to the order/invoice id) and send it on every retry of that attempt — Stripe and most processors dedupe on it, making retries safe.
- On timeout, don't immediately retry — reconcile first: query the processor for that idempotency key/charge to see if it actually succeeded, then only retry if it genuinely didn't go through.
- Only retry on transport-level failures (timeout, 5xx, connection reset). A real decline is a terminal failure — retrying that just confuses the customer.
- Do this out of the request path: mark the charge "processing," retry with bounded attempts and backoff in a background job, and only surface "payment failed" after retries are exhausted or a genuine decline comes back.

The fork that matters: whether the customer-facing flow can tolerate an async "processing" state (webhook/poll to confirm) or needs a synchronous answer within the request — that decision drives whether this is a queue+job or a tight in-request retry loop with a short timeout budget. Left out: the specific backoff schedule and how the webhook reconciliation is wired up, both of which depend on your processor and current architecture.

For a few-word query matching name/description, the fork is exact-keyword vs. fuzzy/typo-tolerant search.

Recommend Postgres full-text search (`tsvector`/`tsquery` with a GIN index) if the catalog is already in Postgres and typo-tolerance isn't critical — no new infra, ranks by relevance, handles "a few words" well. If you need typo tolerance, prefix-as-you-type, or the catalog is large (100k+ products) and Postgres FTS starts feeling slow, use a dedicated search engine like Typesense or Meilisearch instead of building ranking/tokenization by hand.

Second fork: keep the index in sync via a write-through update on product save vs. batch reindex — write-through if search results need to reflect edits immediately, batch if near-real-time is fine.

Left out: ranking tuning (boosting name matches over description), synonyms/stemming, and pagination/faceting — those are the next layer down once the base engine is picked.

- **Resize before or after upload.** Phone camera originals run 5-20MB (HEIC/JPEG) and sellers are often on cellular. Skipping this and resizing server-side after upload is simpler to build but means slow, failure-prone uploads on weak connections.

The current `charge()` has no retry, and `checkout.js` maps every failure — including a timeout — straight to `502 "payment failed"`. - **Key stability**: the idempotency key must be generated once per logical charge (the order), not per HTTP attempt — otherwise each retry looks like a brand-new charge to the vendor and the safety guarantee is gone.

Left out: what to tell the customer if all retries are exhausted and the outcome is still unknown — showing "payment failed" there is still wrong, since a background reconciliation (e.g. a job that re-sends the same idempotency key later, or polls the vendor for that key) is what resolves it, not the request/response cycle.

Left out: keeping the index in sync with product edits (a trigger-updated tsvector column for the in-DB route, or a queue/CDC feed if you go external).

Two decisions actually fork this:

1. **Edge vs. app-level enforcement.** Edge (nginx `limit_req`, Envoy, Kong, cloud gateway) stops the abusive client before it burns app resources — that's the whole point here — but needs infra changes. App-level middleware is easier to ship but only protects if backed by shared state across replicas.
2. **Flat limit vs. tiered by client/plan.** A flat per-key limit fixes today's problem; tiering by plan is the next layer down if you want higher ceilings for paying clients later.

What's fronting `/v1` right now — nginx, a custom gateway, or is the app taking requests directly?

Polling — not WebSockets or SSE. `PLATFORM.md` rules both out: connection upgrades 501 at the edge, and instances freeze/get killed at 10s so nothing can hold a connection open server-side anyway.

Since `rollup.md` says the data only changes once a minute, replace the click handler in `public/dashboard.js` with a `setInterval` calling `load()`, and use the `computed_at` already returned by `/api/metrics` to skip re-rendering when the tick didn't produce new data. `/api/metrics` is already cheap (30ms, 4KB, no-store) so hitting it every 15-20s is fine.

- **Poll cadence**: a fixed interval (simple) vs. aligning requests just after each minute boundary (fewer wasted polls, but needs clock-skew tolerance since the job runs "on the minute" server-side, not client-side).
- **Change detection**: re-render unconditionally each poll vs. compare `computed_at` to the last-seen value and only touch the DOM when it moved.
