The core fix isn't "add a retry loop" — it's not showing failure until you actually know it's failed, plus making retries safe.

**Idempotency key first.** Generate one key per checkout attempt (e.g. order ID) and pass it to the payment provider on every retry. Without this, retrying a timed-out charge risks double-charging if the original actually went through on the processor's side despite the timeout.

**Classify the error before deciding to retry.** A timeout or 5xx/network error is retryable; a decline (insufficient funds, fraud block, expired card) is not — retrying those just wastes time and won't change the outcome. Only the timeout/network bucket should trigger automatic retry.

**Move the retry out of the request path.** Instead of the customer's request blocking through N attempts, mark the charge `pending`, return that state to the UI ("processing," not "failed"), and let a background job (or the provider's own webhook confirming final status) retry with backoff (e.g. a few attempts over 30-60s). Update the order to `succeeded`/`failed` when it resolves, and only then show the customer a real failure.

**Guard against duplicate work**, keyed on the idempotency key: don't let two retry attempts (a manual customer retry and your background job) fire concurrently for the same order.

The fork that actually shapes the implementation: is a background job/queue already in your stack, or would this need to stay synchronous with inline retries (accept the request hanging longer) — which one fits your current infrastructure?

For a few-word query matching name/description, the fork is data scale: under ~100k products, Postgres full-text search (`tsvector` column on name+description, GIN index, `websearch_to_tsquery` with `ts_rank` weighting name higher than description) is simplest and needs no new infra. Past that, or if you want typo-tolerance and better relevance out of the box, move to a dedicated search engine (Typesense/Meilisearch for quick setup, Elasticsearch/OpenSearch if you already run one) fed by a change-data-capture or on-write sync job.

I'd default to Postgres FTS first since it's reversible — swapping to a dedicated engine later just means adding a sync pipeline, not re-architecting the write path. Left out: ranking/relevance tuning, autocomplete-as-you-type, and synonym handling — worth scoping once you know real query patterns.

Recommended shape: client uploads directly to object storage via a short-lived presigned URL (server only issues the URL and records a pending image row), skipping the app server as a byte-proxy. Before upload, downscale/re-encode in the browser/app (e.g. cap the long edge around 2000px, re-encode as JPEG/WebP) — phone photos run 4-12MB at resolutions no listing page needs, and compressing client-side cuts upload time and storage cost. After the object lands, an async job (S3 event, queue, whatever your stack uses) fixes EXIF orientation, strips EXIF/location metadata, and generates a thumbnail; the listing shows the image once that job flips it from pending to ready.

Two decisions actually fork this:
- **Direct-to-storage vs. proxy through your backend** — proxying is simpler to build but doubles bandwidth cost and puts your server in the hot path for every photo.
- **Sync vs. async post-processing** — doing EXIF/thumbnail work inline blocks the upload response; async means the UI needs a pending/ready state for each photo.

Left out: multi-photo ordering/reordering UI, retry/resume for flaky mobile uploads, and storage cleanup for abandoned listings — all straightforward once the above is in place, but depend on your stack, which I don't have visibility into here (no repo present).

**Data-layer cache (Redis), not full-page cache** — read-through on the product query, keyed by `product:{id}`, invalidated on write.

The two decisions that actually matter here:

- **Invalidation**: explicit invalidation when a product record changes (via the write path or a DB change-stream), backed by a short TTL (minutes) as a safety net for anything that slips through — not TTL-only, which gives you a stale-data window you can't bound.
- **What to cache**: the query result, not the rendered page. If any part of the page is per-user (stock check, personalized price, cart state), a full-page/CDN cache will serve stale or wrong personalization; caching just the DB-backed data keeps rendering dynamic while removing the 900ms cost. If the page is genuinely the same for every visitor, CDN edge caching of the full HTML is the bigger win and makes the Redis layer redundant.

Left out: single-flight/lock-on-miss to avoid a thundering herd when a hot key expires, and cache warming — worth designing once you pick the invalidation approach above.

Recommendation: enforce it at the edge (API gateway/load balancer), not in application code — a token-bucket limiter keyed by client (API key, not IP) with counters in Redis so all instances share state, returning 429 + `Retry-After` when a client exceeds its quota.

Two decisions that actually fork the design:
- **Where to enforce**: gateway-level stops the abusive traffic before it burns app/DB capacity (fixes the "degrading everybody else" problem directly); app-level middleware is easier to ship but the request has already cost you CPU/DB time by the time you reject it.
- **Algorithm**: token bucket tolerates legitimate bursts while capping sustained rate; fixed-window counters are simpler but let a client double their burst at window boundaries. Sliding-window-log is more precise but costlier — usually not worth it here.

Left out: per-tier limit values, how to identify/authenticate the client, and whether to add a global circuit breaker as a backstop — that's the next layer down once the mechanism is picked.

Given the constraints in `PLATFORM.md`: WebSocket upgrades are rejected at the edge (501), functions are killed at 10s, and there's no sticky routing or shared memory across instances — so no persistent connection (WebSocket or SSE) can survive between requests. That rules out real push entirely; polling is the only option this platform supports.

The data itself only changes once a minute anyway (`jobs/rollup.md`: the rollup job is the sole writer, on a fixed schedule tied to the finance close window). So build it as `setInterval` in `public/dashboard.js` calling the existing `load()` on something like a 15–20s cadence — frequent enough that staleness stays under a minute, infrequent enough not to hammer `/api/metrics` for no reason, since `computed_at` won't move between rollups anyway. Drop the click-only "Refresh" listener; the interval replaces it (`refresh` button can stay as a manual force-check or go away).

One level down: pause the interval on `visibilitychange` so backgrounded tabs stop polling, and skip the DOM re-render when `computed_at` is unchanged from the last fetch.

The real bug: a timeout means *unknown*, not *failed* — the charge may have gone through processor-side. Retrying blindly risks a double charge, so that has to be solved first.

**Build it as:**
1. **Idempotency key** per charge attempt (e.g. order ID + attempt number), sent to the processor, so any retry of the same logical charge dedupes on their end instead of creating a second charge.
2. **Retry only on ambiguous/transient errors** — timeout, 5xx, network drop — never on declines (insufficient funds, fraud block), which are terminal and just pollute the retry logic.
3. **Explicit charge state** (pending/succeeded/failed) stored per attempt, not inferred from the last HTTP response, so a late webhook can resolve a stuck "pending" instead of the system assuming failure.
4. **Reconciliation before retry**: on timeout, query the processor for that idempotency key's actual status (short backoff, e.g. 2s/5s/15s) before either retrying or declaring failure.

**The fork that matters most:** inline retry in the request path (customer waits a few extra seconds on a spinner) vs. async — return "processing" immediately, retry/reconcile in a background job, flip the UI via webhook once resolved. Since customers currently see a hard "failed" on what's often a transient blip, moving to "processing" + async resolution is the bigger fix, not just adding retries. Say the word if you want that job/webhook flow designed in detail.

Left out: backoff count/cutoff before a "pending" becomes a real failure, and what happens to charges still stuck past that cutoff (manual review vs. auto-void).

Postgres full-text search, not a separate search service — 38K rows and a single Postgres instance don't justify standing up Elasticsearch/OpenSearch.

Add a generated `tsvector` column on `products` weighting `name` above `description`, index it with GIN, and query with `websearch_to_tsquery` ordered by `ts_rank`. That's a migration plus a new route in `routes/products.js` alongside the existing `/` and `/:id` handlers.

The fork: exact/prefix matching (typo-tolerant, "iphon" matches nothing) vs. trigram similarity (`pg_trgm`) for fuzzy/typo tolerance. Given users "type a few words," full-text search covers word-level matching well; trigram would layer on top later if typo-tolerance becomes a complaint. I'd ship plain full-text search first and add trigram only if needed — that's the depth I'd leave for a follow-up rather than build now.

The two decisions that actually shape this:

**Upload path**: have the client request a presigned URL and upload straight to object storage (S3/GCS/R2), not through your app server. Phone photos run 3-8MB each and sellers often add several at once — proxying that through your API wastes server bandwidth and memory for no benefit.

**Where resizing happens**: downscale client-side before upload (canvas-based, cap long edge around 2000px) to cut upload time on cellular, then do the authoritative processing server-side after upload completes — strip EXIF (GPS/orientation), generate thumbnail + listing-size variants via a background job. Create the listing photo row in `pending` state on upload start, flip to `ready` when the job finishes, so the seller's submit isn't blocked on processing.

Left out: how you handle failed/abandoned uploads (orphaned storage objects) and moderation/content scanning — worth a follow-up once the storage and job pieces are settled.

The 900ms is almost entirely `relatedProducts` (600ms) and `stockFor` (250ms) in `db.js`, and `/p` is anonymous and identical for every visitor — but `middleware/security.js` sets `no-store` app-wide as a blanket fix for an account-page leak, so the CDN sitting in front of you (0% hit rate, respects origin headers, no path rules) never gets a chance to cache it.

The fix is a header change, not a new caching layer: scope `security.js` so `/account` keeps `no-store` (that's the actual audit finding) and `/p` instead sends `Cache-Control: public, max-age=<catalog-edit-interval>` — the CDN already does the rest, for free, at the edge.

The one real fork: `stockFor` isn't a slow catalog read, it's inventory that moves on a different cadence than "product edited in admin a few times a day." Baking it into the same cached HTML means either stale stock or a TTL too short to help the 600ms join. Pull stock out of the cached response — fetch it client-side after the cached shell loads, or serve it from its own short-TTL/no-cache endpoint — so the expensive part (product + related) can cache for hours while stock stays live.

Rate limit by `client_id`, not IP — the auth middleware comment in `routes/api.js` notes clients share NATs and use multiple addresses, so IP-keying would throttle innocent neighbors and miss the actual offender.

The fork that matters: where the counter lives. `app.js` clusters 4 workers per box with nothing shared in-process, so an in-memory limiter (e.g. `express-rate-limit`'s default store) would only cap each worker independently — a client could burst 4x by hitting different workers. `redis.js` already gives you the one thing every worker and every box shares, so put the counter there: `INCR ratelimit:{client_id}:{window}` with `EXPIRE`, or a small Lua script if you want token-bucket smoothing instead of hard window edges. `api_keys.plan` is already fetched in the auth middleware, so limits can vary by plan for free.

Enforce it right in that same middleware in `routes/api.js`, immediately after `req.client` is set and before the route handlers touch Postgres — reject with `429` and a `Retry-After` header so the offending client backs off instead of retrying immediately.

Depth left out: exact algorithm (fixed window vs. sliding log vs. token bucket) and limit values per plan.

Poll from the client — the platform rules out anything push-based: `api/` functions can't accept a WebSocket upgrade (hard 501 at the edge per PLATFORM.md), and instances are frozen between invocations, so nothing can hold a connection or timer open server-side to push updates. That's the one fork that actually matters here; there's no server-sent-events or socket option to weigh against it.

Given polling is forced, the only real design decision left is the interval, and the rollup job in `jobs/rollup.md` settles that too: the data changes at most once a minute, on the minute. So `public/dashboard.js` would `setInterval(load, ...)` at something like 15–20s, and `load()` would compare the new `computed_at` against the last-rendered one, skipping `render()` when it's unchanged — cheap given `api/metrics.js` already returns `computed_at` and the response is 4KB/30ms with `no-store`, so there's no caching layer to add.

Left out: exponential backoff / pause-when-tab-hidden polish, which is a follow-up, not a fork.

Retrying here is safe only because Cardstream supports idempotency keys — the risk isn't "will the retry go through," it's double-charging on a request that actually succeeded before timing out. `payments.js:5` doesn't send `Idempotency-Key` at all right now, so that's the real gap, not the lack of a retry loop.

**Design:**

1. **Persist an idempotency key on the order before the first charge attempt**, not generate one per call. Add a column (e.g. `orders.payment_attempt_key`), set it once when the order enters checkout, and reuse it for every attempt against that order — including if the whole request times out and the customer/browser hits "pay" again. A key generated inside `charge()` and thrown away on failure doesn't protect against that second, separate HTTP request to `/pay`.

2. **Retry only on timeout/network errors, not on 4xx declines.** A card decline is a real, known outcome — retrying it just re-declines. Only the "unknown" outcomes (`req.on("timeout")`, `req.on("error")` in `payments.js:36-37`) are retry-eligible per `PROVIDER.md`.

3. **Bounded retry with backoff inside `charge()`**, same idempotency key on every attempt: a few tries (e.g. 3), short jittered backoff between them. Rate limit is 600/min so there's no throttling concern.

4. **If retries are exhausted, don't tell the customer "failed."** The outcome is still unknown, not declined. Surface it as a distinct state (e.g. order stays `pending_payment` or moves to `payment_unknown`) rather than `checkout.js:31`'s blanket `502 "payment failed"`, and reconcile later by charging with the same idempotency key (safe, returns the original result) or querying the charge status.

The fork that matters most: whether the idempotency key lives on the order (survives across separate `/pay` requests) or only inside a single `charge()` call (only survives in-process retries). Given the customer can just click pay again after seeing "failed," it needs to be on the order.

**Recommendation:** index `name`+`description` with Postgres full-text search (a generated `tsvector` column + GIN index, ranked with `ts_rank`) if the catalog's already in Postgres and under a few million rows — no new infrastructure, good enough relevance for short queries.

Two decisions actually fork this:
- **Sync strategy** — a trigger-maintained `tsvector` column keeps search always current but couples index updates to every write; a scheduled/async reindex job decouples them at the cost of staleness. Pick based on how fast products change.
- **Typo-tolerance / prefix-as-you-type** — plain Postgres FTS matches whole tokens/stems, not misspellings or partial words. If the UI needs "so tumbler" to match "soft tumbler" while typing, add `pg_trgm` for fuzzy matching, or skip Postgres FTS entirely and use a dedicated engine (Meilisearch/Typesense are the low-ops choice; Elasticsearch/OpenSearch if you need more tuning) — at the cost of running and syncing a separate service.

If the catalog is large (tens of millions+) or relevance quality is a top priority, skip straight to the dedicated search engine.

Direct-to-storage with presigned URLs, plus client-side resize before upload. Server checks listing ownership and a photo-count cap, issues a short-lived presigned PUT URL, the client uploads straight to S3/GCS, then confirms completion to the API, which writes the photo row (status: uploaded) and enqueues async thumbnail/variant generation off a bucket event — nothing heavy happens inline on the request.

Before that PUT, resize/compress in the browser with a canvas (downscale to ~2048px longest edge, JPEG quality ~0.8). That's the piece that matters most for phone camera photos specifically: a 4-12MB HEIC/JPEG becomes a few hundred KB, which is the difference between a listing upload working and stalling on cellular.

Two decisions actually fork this design:

1. Presigned direct-to-storage vs. proxying uploads through your app server. Proxying is simpler if object storage isn't wired up yet, but it doubles bandwidth and ties up server workers on slow mobile uploads.
2. Client-side compression vs. accepting raw files and compressing server-side. Client-side saves the upload bandwidth/time itself but adds JS complexity and inconsistent output across phone browsers; server-side is uniform but costs latency/bandwidth on large originals.

Left out: resumable/retry handling for flaky mobile connections, EXIF orientation correction, and moderation/virus scanning on upload.

Cache the assembled product data (price, stock, description, etc.), not raw HTML, in Redis keyed by product ID (+ variant/locale if applicable), with the DB queries replaced by a cache-read-through on miss.

The fork that matters: how you invalidate.
- **TTL-only** (e.g., 60s): trivial to add, zero coupling to write paths, but stale price/stock for up to the TTL window.
- **Write-invalidation**: on product update/price/stock change, delete or refresh the key — fresh data, but you have to find and touch every write path (admin UI, bulk import, inventory sync) that can mutate a cached product.

Pick write-invalidation with a longer TTL (minutes) as a backstop for any write path you miss — stale prices are the kind of bug that erodes trust, and 900ms→DB is expensive enough that a pure short TTL undersells the win.

Key fork: rate limit by `client_id`, not IP — the auth middleware in `routes/api.js:9-19` already resolves `req.client.client_id` from the API key, and the comment there notes clients share IPs (NAT) and use multiple IPs, so IP-based limiting would both under- and over-block.

Second fork: where the counter lives. `app.js` runs 4 clustered workers per box with separate heaps (line 6's comment), so an in-process counter won't see the abusive client's full request rate. `redis.js` is already the one store shared by every worker on every box — reuse that connection for a per-`client_id` counter (atomic INCR + PEXPIRE, or a small Lua script if you want token-bucket smoothing instead of hard window-boundary bursts).

Wire it as a `router.use` in `routes/api.js` right after the auth middleware (so it has `req.client`) and before the route handlers, returning 429 with `Retry-After` when exceeded — that also shields Postgres from the hammering. Since `api_keys.plan` is already selected, limits can vary by plan without extra schema work.

Left out: exact limits/tiers, and whether to cap by request rate alone or also by concurrency — that's a follow-up decision once you know the traffic pattern.

Poll, not push — the platform rules out anything else. `PLATFORM.md` says WebSocket handshakes 501 at the edge and instances are frozen between invocations, so SSE/WebSockets can't hold a connection open here even in principle. And it doesn't cost you anything: `rollup.md` says the data only changes once a minute, so sub-minute realtime isn't actually a goal.

Concretely: in `public/dashboard.js`, replace the click-only trigger with `setInterval(load, 20000)` (or similar), calling the same `/api/metrics` endpoint — it's already stateless and cheap (30ms, 4KB), which is exactly the shape serverless functions want. No backend change needed.

The one real fork: pick a poll interval relative to the 1-minute rollup cadence — something like 15-30s gives freshness without tripling request volume for no benefit, since polling faster than the data changes just wastes calls.

Left out: pausing polling when the tab is hidden (`document.visibilitychange`) and skipping re-render when `computed_at` is unchanged, to avoid needless flicker/CPU on an inactive tab.

The core risk: a timeout means you don't know if the charge succeeded on the processor's side, so a naive retry can double-charge. Build it around that, not around "try again":

- **Idempotency key per attempt** — generate one before the first request and reuse it on every retry of that same charge. Stripe/most processors dedupe on it, so a retry either returns the original result or safely creates one charge.
- **Reconcile before retrying** — on timeout, query the processor for that key's actual status instead of assuming failure. Only enqueue a retry if it comes back genuinely failed or still unresolved.
- **Retry out of the request path** — the original HTTP call already timed out, so retries belong in a background job/queue with backoff and a max attempt count, not a loop in the handler.
- **Fix the customer-facing state** — a timeout should show "processing," not "payment failed"; flip it to success/failure once reconciliation or a webhook confirms the real outcome.

The two decisions that actually fork the design: whether you can pass a stable idempotency key to your processor (if not, dedup has to happen on your side via a charge-attempt ledger), and whether you reconcile via polling or via webhook — webhook is less code to run repeatedly but adds a dependency on the processor delivering it reliably. Left out: backoff schedule tuning and the queue/worker choice, which are implementation detail once the above is settled.

At 38k rows, Postgres full-text search is the right call — no need for Elasticsearch/Algolia here. Add a generated `tsvector` column over `name` and `description` with a GIN index, query it with `websearch_to_tsquery` and rank with `ts_rank`, in a new `GET /products/search?q=` route alongside the existing paged listing in `routes/products.js`.

If typo-tolerance matters for your users, add `pg_trgm` with a GIN index on `name` and blend it in (or fall back to it when full-text returns zero rows) — more moving parts, worth it only if search-abandonment is a concern you actually have data on.

Direct-to-storage upload with client-side compression, backend only handling metadata:

**Client**: On photo select, downscale/compress in the browser (canvas or `createImageBitmap` + resize to ~2000px longest edge, JPEG ~80%) before upload — phone camera photos run 3-8MB/12MP+, and sellers often add several per listing, so this cuts upload time and storage cost dramatically with no visible quality loss at listing-photo sizes. Strip EXIF (GPS especially — sellers photographing from home don't want location leaked).

**Transfer**: Backend issues a short-lived presigned upload URL (S3/GCS/R2) per photo; client uploads directly to object storage rather than proxying bytes through your app server. Backend then gets a webhook/callback or the client confirms completion, and a row (listing_id, storage_key, order, status) gets written to the photos table.

**Processing**: Async job (queue-triggered on upload-complete) generates a few sizes — thumbnail, listing-card, full-view — since serving a full-res original to every browsing user wastes bandwidth. Store the derived URLs, not the raw upload, as what the UI renders.

**Mobile-specific forks worth deciding now**:
- HEIC from iPhones — decode/convert client-side (many browsers can't render HEIC) or accept it and convert server-side. Client-side avoids a broken-image state before processing finishes.
- Flaky connections — chunked/resumable upload (S3 multipart or tus) if listings routinely fail partway; skip it if photos are already small post-compression.

That's the shape; specifics like max photo count per listing and reordering UI are the next layer down.

The 900ms is avoidable for repeat traffic, and the CDN already sitting in front (`CDN.md`) is the tool for it — this is blocked by a policy bug, not a missing layer. `middleware/security.js` sets `no-store` app-wide because of a 2024 finding that `/account` (genuinely per-user, reads `req.session.userId`) leaked through an intermediary cache. That fix was scoped to the wrong blast radius: it also hits `/p/:slug`, which reads no session, is identical for every visitor, and only changes when the catalog is edited a few times a day. Right now the CDN has a 0% hit rate solely because this shared middleware tells it not to cache anything.

**Fix**: stop applying one `Cache-Control` policy to every route. Keep `/account` exactly as-is (`no-store, no-cache, must-revalidate, private`; keep `X-Frame-Options`/`nosniff` on both). Give `/p` a real shared-cache directive, e.g. `Cache-Control: public, s-maxage=300, stale-while-revalidate=60` — `s-maxage` because the CDN is a shared cache, no `Vary: Cookie` needed since nothing on the page varies by user. That alone takes repeat product-page requests off the database entirely, with no new caching infrastructure required, since the CDN already honors whatever the origin sends.

One real fork: TTL length trades hit rate against stock staleness, since `stockFor` (~250ms) is baked into the same cached page as the ~600ms `relatedProducts` join. Either accept a few minutes of stale stock count (it's advisory, not re-checked at checkout) and cache the whole page, or split stock into its own low-TTL/uncached fragment so the expensive join gets the long TTL while stock stays near-live. First hits and post-invalidation misses still pay the full 900ms — an origin-side cache (e.g. Redis keyed by product id, invalidated when the admin tool publishes) is the next layer down if that gap matters.

Rate-limit on `client_id`, not IP — the auth middleware in `routes/api.js:9-19` already resolves that from the API key before hitting the routes, and the comment right above it flags that clients share NAT addresses, so IP-keying would either miss the offender or punish their neighbors. Enforce it as one more check in that same middleware, right after `req.client` is set: atomically `INCR` a `ratelimit:{client_id}:{window}` key in the Redis client already in `redis.js` (shared across all boxes/workers — the cluster setup in `app.js` gives each worker its own heap, so an in-process counter would only see 1/4 of that client's traffic per box), set an expiry on first increment, and return 429 with `Retry-After` once the count exceeds the plan's limit.

The one real fork: fixed-window `INCR`+`EXPIRE` vs. a token bucket. The counter is simpler and enough to stop one client from drowning out everyone else; a token bucket is worth the extra complexity only if you also want to let clients burst above their average rate without tripping the limit. Left out: per-route limits and sliding-window-log precision at the window edges — neither matters until the blunt per-client cap turns out insufficient.

Recommendation: server-sent events (SSE) from the backend, pushing new data whenever it changes, with the client re-rendering on receipt — no polling loop. SSE is simpler than WebSockets for one-way updates and works over plain HTTP.

Two decisions actually fork the design:

1. **How the backend knows something changed.** Either it recomputes on a timer and pushes if the value differs (simple, adds a delay up to the timer interval), or it pushes on the actual write (e.g., a DB trigger, a pub/sub message from whatever job updates the metrics). Timer-based is far less work to build; event-driven is only worth it if updates are latency-sensitive.

2. **Push transport.** SSE if updates only flow server-to-client (the dashboard's case). WebSockets only if the client also needs to send commands back (e.g., acknowledging alerts, changing filters that affect server-side computation).

Fallback: keep a manual refresh button and have the client poll on reconnect, since SSE connections drop on network hiccups and need reconnect logic anyway (`EventSource` does this automatically).

The core problem isn't "retry the request" — a timeout means you don't know whether the charge went through on the processor's side, so retrying blindly risks double-charging. The design has to be built around that uncertainty:

1. **Idempotency key per charge attempt**, generated once (e.g. at checkout/order id) and reused on every retry of that same logical charge. Any processor worth using (Stripe, Braintree, Adyen) will dedupe on this key, so a resent request either returns the original result or safely creates the charge once.
2. **Reconcile before retrying**, not after. On timeout, first query the processor for the status of that idempotency key/charge rather than immediately firing a new attempt — the original request may have completed on their end even though your response never arrived.
3. **Bounded retry with backoff**, run from a queue/worker rather than inline in the request path, since the customer-facing request already timed out once and shouldn't be held open through multiple retries.
4. **Only surface "payment failed" after retries + reconciliation are exhausted**, and distinguish that from a hard decline (which should never be retried).

The fork that actually matters: whether retries happen synchronously in the request/response cycle (simpler, but the customer waits) or asynchronously via a background job that updates order status and notifies the customer once resolved (better UX for a few-times-a-day timeout rate, more moving parts). Given this is a rare intermittent timeout rather than a hot path, async reconciliation is the better fit.

Two decisions actually fork the design:

1. **Invalidation** — TTL-only (say 60s, simplest, accepts brief staleness) vs. event-driven (bust the key when the product's updated/price changes, needs the write path to publish that). For a product page, TTL plus explicit invalidation on writes is the usual pick: fast to build, and you don't serve a stale price for a full TTL window after an edit.
2. **Granularity** — cache the whole assembled page payload as one blob, vs. caching the volatile pieces (price, inventory) separately from the stable ones (description, images) with different TTLs. On exceeding the bucket, return 429 with a `Retry-After` header instead of dropping/hanging the connection.

Two decisions actually fork this; the rest is standard plumbing.

**The one non-negotiable piece:** every charge attempt needs an idempotency key, generated once per order/invoice, reused across retries. Without it, retrying a timed-out charge risks double-charging the customer if the original request actually succeeded downstream and only the response was lost.

**Design:**
- Classify the failure before deciding to retry: timeouts/network errors/5xx are retryable (ambiguous outcome); declines/insufficient funds are not (definite outcome — show the real reason immediately, don't retry).
- On a retryable failure, don't mark the charge "failed" — mark it "processing" and enqueue a background retry with exponential backoff + jitter, capped at a few attempts over a couple minutes.
- Only flip the customer-facing status to failed once retries are exhausted or a non-retryable error comes back; update the UI via webhook/poll rather than blocking the original request.

**The two forks:**
1. Where the key is generated — client-side (survives a page refresh or double-click, so a resubmit reuses the same key) vs server-side per request (simpler but vulnerable to duplicate submits creating separate charges). Client-side is the safer default.
2. Retry timing — inline/synchronous (hold the request open a few seconds, simplest, but ties up the request thread and still risks a second timeout) vs async job queue with the UI polling/webhook for the final state (more moving parts, but doesn't block and handles the "few times a day" volume cleanly). Async is the better fit given the failure is already sporadic and timeout-driven.

Left out: queue/backoff tech choice, exact retry counts, and reconciliation logic for attempts where you truly can't tell if the charge landed — those are next-level-down details once the two forks above are picked.

The 900ms isn't a caching gap you need to fill from scratch — it's a caching opportunity you're currently blocking. `CDN.md` says the edge already fronts every request and honors whatever `Cache-Control` the origin sends, but `middleware/security.js` sets `no-store, no-cache, private` on *every* route, including `/p`. Hit rate is 0% because of that header, not because the CDN can't do the job. `routes/products.js` confirms `/p/:slug` is fully anonymous — no session read, nothing per-user — so it never needed that policy; only `/account` did, per the audit comment.

**Recommendation:** stop applying `security.js`'s Cache-Control blanket app-wide; scope it per route.
- `/account` keeps `no-store, no-cache, must-revalidate, private` exactly as-is — that's the actual audit requirement.
- `/p` instead sends something like `Cache-Control: public, max-age=30, stale-while-revalidate=300`. A CDN hit serves the page with zero origin work, which is the only way to erase 900ms of DB time — an app-level cache still pays full render cost per request; an edge hit pays none.

**The one real fork:** freshness per query, since they don't age at the same rate. `db.js`'s comments say catalog data (`productBySlug`, `relatedProducts`) changes "a few times a day," so a multi-minute page TTL is safe. `stockFor` is inventory and can't tolerate the same staleness without an overselling risk. Two ways to handle that: give the whole page a short TTL bounded by stock's tolerance (wastes the cacheability of the 600ms `relatedProducts` join), or pull stock out of the cached HTML and have the client hit a separate, short-TTL/uncached endpoint for it — letting the expensive join get the long cache win without stock going stale for minutes.

Left out: purge wiring (does the admin tool invalidate the CDN path on save, or rely on TTL alone), stampede protection when a hot slug's entry expires, and whether an app-level cache (Redis in front of `relatedProducts`/`stockFor`) is worth adding for the requests that still reach origin — a second-order optimization once the edge is actually being used.

On exceeding the bucket, return `429` with a `Retry-After` header rather than dropping/hanging the connection.

If it's horizontally scaled, in-memory limiting per instance lets a client multiply their effective quota by hitting different instances, so you need a shared store (Redis, incrementing counters via a Lua script for atomicity) that all instances check against — at the cost of a network round-trip per request and a new dependency to keep available.

Left out: whether to pause polling on `visibilitychange` when the tab is backgrounded, and retry/backoff behavior if a poll fails.

The current code has no retry at all — `payments.js` line 5 says so explicitly, and `checkout.js` catches every error, including a timeout, and reports it to the customer as "payment failed." `PROVIDER.md` says the vendor treats a timed-out charge as **unknown, not failed** — the request may have gone through. So today's real bug is that a naive retry (or even the current no-retry failure message) could easily double-charge a customer, since `payments.js` never sends the `Idempotency-Key` header the vendor supports.

**Recommendation:** generate an idempotency key that's stable per logical charge attempt (e.g. the order id, or an id on a `charge_attempts` row created before the first call — not a fresh UUID per HTTP request), send it on every attempt including retries, and on timeout leave the order in a `processing` state rather than `failed`. Retry asynchronously — a background job or queue worker, not inline in the route handler — replaying the same idempotency key with backoff and a capped attempt count, until it gets a definitive result (paid, or a genuine decline) and updates the order.

Two decisions actually fork this:

- **Inline vs. async retry.** Retrying inline in `checkout.js` while the customer waits is tempting but doesn't solve the problem: stacking a few 10s timeouts makes the request itself slow, and if the retry also times out you're back to "unknown" with nothing left to do but respond. Async lets you return "processing" immediately and keep retrying in the background until you have a real answer.
- **What the idempotency key is derived from.** It has to survive across separate retry attempts (possibly separate processes), so it can't be generated fresh each call — order id or a persisted attempt id is what makes the "same key = same charge" guarantee actually hold.

Left out: backoff/attempt-limit tuning, how the customer learns the final outcome (webhook, poll endpoint, or email), and a periodic sweep for orders stuck in `processing` if the retry worker itself dies mid-attempt.

Postgres full-text search: a generated `tsvector` column over `name || description`, a GIN index, ranked with `ts_rank`. No new infra, and it's plenty fast up to low millions of rows — reasonable default unless you already know otherwise.

The real fork is catalog size/features: if you need typo tolerance, faceted filters, or sub-50ms at scale, skip Postgres and use a dedicated engine like Typesense or Meilisearch (self-hosted, easy) instead. That also changes the sync story — Postgres FTS updates in the same transaction via a trigger; an external engine needs a separate indexing pipeline (CDC or a periodic job) to keep it current with writes.

Left out at this level: relevance weighting (name vs. description), synonym/typo handling, and pagination/highlighting — worth a pass once you pick the backend.

2. **Granularity.** A single global "abusive client" limit is simplest, but if `/v1` has expensive vs. cheap endpoints, consider per-route or weighted-cost limits so one client can't burn the whole budget hitting the priciest call.

Two decisions that actually fork the design:
- **Push vs. poll**: if the backend can't cheaply detect changes (no triggers/CDC/pub-sub on the data source), short-interval polling (5-15s) is simpler and often indistinguishable from push for a dashboard.
- **How the server learns data changed**: either the write path publishes an event (DB trigger, outbox, message queue) that fans out to connected clients, or the server just re-queries on a timer and diffs against the last snapshot before pushing.

Left out: reconnect/backoff handling, auth on long-lived connections, and horizontal scaling of the push fan-out (needs a shared pub/sub like Redis if there's more than one server instance) — worth another pass once you pick push vs. poll.

The fix is treating a timeout as *unknown*, not *failed* — right now it sounds like a timeout is being mapped straight to a decline.

1. **Idempotency key per charge attempt**, generated once per order and reused on every retry. This is what makes retrying safe at all — without it a retry after a timeout can double-charge the customer.
2. **On timeout, check status before retrying.** Query the provider for that idempotency key (Stripe and most processors support this) rather than blindly resubmitting — the original call may have actually succeeded on their end even though your request timed out.
3. **Retry only on retryable errors** (timeout, 5xx, network) with bounded exponential backoff, e.g. 3 attempts. Never retry a genuine decline (insufficient funds, fraud block, etc.) — that's a real failure, not a transient one.
4. **Only show "payment failed" after retries are exhausted and the provider returns an actual decline.** While retrying, the customer should see "processing," not "failed."

The fork that matters: **inline retry** (do the retries synchronously within the request, simplest to build, but the customer's request stays open a few extra seconds) vs. **async retry via a queue** (return "processing" immediately, retry in the background, notify the customer via webhook/poll when resolved). Pick inline if timeouts resolve in a couple seconds; pick async if they can take longer or you want the request path to stay fast.

Left out: exact backoff schedule, where charge-attempt state gets persisted for the status check, and webhook wiring for the async path.

Two decisions actually fork the design: keyword vs. semantic (embedding-based) ranking — embeddings handle synonyms and loose intent better but add an embedding pipeline and vector index — and whether the search index updates in real time or via periodic batch sync from the product catalog.

Depends on one thing: are these pages personalized (per-user price, inventory, cart state) or the same HTML for everyone?

- **Not personalized** — put a reverse-proxy/CDN cache in front of the whole rendered page, keyed by product slug, with a short TTL (or none) plus purge-on-update. This is the biggest win since it skips your app entirely, not just the DB.
- **Personalized** — cache can't sit at the edge; put a read-through cache (Redis) around the DB queries themselves, keyed by product id, with the same TTL + invalidate-on-write pattern. The page still renders per-request, but the 900ms mostly disappears.

Key by `client_id`, not IP — `routes/api.js` already notes clients share addresses behind NAT and one client uses many, so IP buckets would throttle innocent tenants sharing a NAT and miss the offender rotating addresses.

Enforce it as Redis-backed middleware inserted right after the auth block in `routes/api.js` (routes/api.js:18), once `req.client.client_id` and `.plan` are resolved but before the route handlers run. Use the existing `redis.js` client rather than any in-process counter — `app.js` forks 4 worker processes with separate heaps, so an in-memory counter would let each client burst 4x by hitting different workers; Redis is already the one thing shared across workers and boxes.

For the algorithm, the fork is fixed-window `INCR`+`EXPIRE` vs. a sliding-window/token-bucket Lua script: the fixed window is one round-trip and trivial to reason about, but lets a client burst 2x the limit at window boundaries; the Lua-script sliding window costs a bit more Redis CPU but bounds bursts tightly. Given one client is actively hammering you today, go with the sliding-window Lua script — boundary bursts are exactly the kind of gap an aggressive client will find.

Left out: per-plan limit tuning (though `req.client.plan` is already there to key off of), and whether to rate-limit writes (`POST /reports`) more strictly than reads.

Two forking decisions:

**Poll vs. push.** If the underlying data changes at a moderate pace (seconds-to-minutes) and the client count is small-to-moderate, short-interval polling (a `setInterval` fetch every 5-15s) is simplest and often sufficient — no new infra, works through any proxy/load balancer. If updates need to be near-instant or the dashboard has many concurrent viewers, use SSE (server-sent events) for one-way server-to-client push, or WebSockets if the dashboard ever needs to send anything back. SSE is the better default for a pure "display live ops data" case — simpler than WebSockets, auto-reconnects, and plays nicely with HTTP infra.

**Where "changed" gets detected.** Either the server diffs on each request/tick and only pushes deltas, or it re-publishes full state on every change and the client does a cheap re-render. For an ops dashboard, publishing full state on each update is usually fine unless payloads are large — diffing adds complexity you likely don't need yet.

My pick: SSE endpoint that streams state whenever the underlying metrics change (or on a fixed tick if the source doesn't naturally emit events), with the client keeping a single `EventSource` open and replacing state on each message, plus a reconnect/backoff and a "stale data" indicator if the connection drops.

Left out: auth on the stream endpoint, and how far back you replay on reconnect — worth deciding once you know the data source.

The core fix is idempotency, not just retrying — a timeout doesn't tell you whether the charge landed on the processor's side, so blindly retrying risks double-charging the customer.

**Design:**
1. Generate an idempotency key per charge attempt (client-generated, stored with the order) and pass it to the payment processor (Stripe, Braintree, etc. all support this natively). Retrying with the same key is then safe — the processor returns the original result instead of creating a second charge.
2. Classify the failure before deciding to retry: timeouts/5xx/network errors are retryable, declines/insufficient-funds/fraud-blocks are not. Only the first bucket should ever retry.
3. Move the retry off the request path into a background job with backoff (e.g. 3 attempts, exponential), so the checkout request isn't held open. On enqueue, show the customer "processing" rather than "payment failed" — that message should only appear once retries are exhausted or a non-retryable decline comes back.

**The two decisions that actually fork this:**
- Sync quick-retry (1-2 immediate retries before responding) vs. async job queue with a "processing" state and a webhook/callback to finalize the order. Async is more resilient but requires you to handle the customer being gone before resolution (email/notification on final failure).
- Where the idempotency key lives — client-generated at "place order" time (survives page reloads/duplicate submits) vs. server-generated per attempt (simpler, but a retried request from the client can still double-submit).

Left out: webhook reconciliation for charges that succeed after your process gave up waiting, and the exact backoff/attempt-count tuning — depends on your processor's own timeout behavior.

Two forks: where the index lives, and how forgiving matching needs to be.

If products are already in Postgres/MySQL, start with the database's own full-text search (Postgres `tsvector` + GIN index over name+description, name weighted higher via `setweight`) — no new infra, good enough for exact/stemmed word matches. Add `pg_trgm` alongside it if you need typo tolerance or substring matches on partial words. Only reach for a dedicated engine (Typesense/Meilisearch/Elasticsearch) if you need instant-as-you-type latency at scale, faceting, or relevance tuning beyond what Postgres ranking gives you — that's a real infra addition, not a drop-in.

The other decision is indexing strategy: a materialized/generated `tsvector` column updated on write (cheap, simple) versus a separate search index kept in sync via triggers or a queue (needed once you outgrow single-DB search). Start with the generated column; that's the piece worth revisiting if search becomes its own service later.

1. **Where resizing happens.** Downscale/compress client-side before upload (e.g. canvas resize to ~2000px, JPEG quality ~80) — phone originals are often 4-12MB and cell uploads are slow, so this cuts upload time the most. 1. **Invalidation vs TTL-only** — if product data changes rarely and staleness of a few minutes is fine, a short TTL (30–60s) with no explicit invalidation is simplest and avoids bugs from missed invalidation paths. 2. **What you cache** — cache the fully-assembled page data (fewer cache lookups, more memory, must invalidate on any input change) vs. cache individual DB query results (composes naturally, smaller invalidation surface, but the page still does N cache lookups instead of N DB queries).

Key design: identify each caller by API key (or token/IP if no key), and enforce a token-bucket limit per client at the edge — API gateway or reverse proxy — before requests reach /v1. Two decisions fork this:

**Push vs. poll.** If updates are frequent (multiple/minute) or you want sub-second latency, use Server-Sent Events (SSE) — simplest to build over plain HTTP, one-directional which is all a dashboard needs, and reconnects automatically in the browser. WebSockets only earn their complexity if the dashboard also needs to send data back (acks, filters that hit the server per keystroke).
