Root cause: the CDN is already in front of every request and honors whatever `Cache-Control` the app sends, but `middleware/security.js` slaps `no-store` on everything app-wide, including `/p` — that's why the edge hit rate is 0%. The DB cost (600ms related + 250ms stock + 40ms lookup) is entirely for anonymous, non-personalized content, which is exactly what that CDN should be absorbing for free.

So: don't build a new cache layer — stop suppressing the one you have. Two decisions actually fork this:

1. **Where the `no-store` header gets set.** It's there because of a real finding (`/account` leaked cross-user), so it can't just be deleted. Move it out of the global `app.use(security)` path and set it explicitly in `account.js` instead, leaving `products.js` free to set its own `Cache-Control: public, max-age=..., stale-while-revalidate=...`. That keeps the audit fix intact while unblocking `/p`.

2. **Whether stock rides along in the same cached response.** Catalog data (product + related, ~640ms) only changes a few times a day, so a page-level TTL of a minute or more is safe. Stock changes on every order, so caching it at the same TTL means selling against stale numbers. Simplest fix: one short shared TTL (30–60s) for the whole page — it still eliminates the vast majority of the 900ms and keeps stock staleness bounded to that window. Only split stock into its own small endpoint (fetched separately, uncached or very-short-TTL) if the business later wants the page TTL longer than stock staleness can tolerate — that's more moving parts (an extra request, partial-page caching at the edge) for a problem you don't have yet.

Pick: fix the middleware scope, add `Cache-Control: public, max-age=60, stale-while-revalidate=300` in `products.js`, leave stock in the same response.

Identify the offending client by API key or account ID, not IP — IP is often shared (NAT, corporate proxies) and trivially rotated. Enforce with a token bucket per client key, counters kept in Redis (or equivalent shared store) so limits hold across all instances, not just one process. Put the check at the edge (API gateway / reverse proxy) so overage requests get rejected with 429 + Retry-After before they ever reach the app servers doing real work.

The fork that actually matters: is there already a gateway/proxy in front of `/v1` (nginx, Envoy, Kong, cloud API gateway)? If so, use its built-in rate limiting rather than hand-rolling middleware — less code, better performance under load. What's currently fronting `/v1`?

Push is off the table here: WebSocket upgrades 501 at the edge, functions freeze after 10s, and there's no sticky routing — nothing can hold a connection open. So this has to be polling, driven from `dashboard.js`.

Since `rollup` only changes once a minute on a fixed schedule (`jobs/rollup.md`), wrap the existing `load()` in a `setInterval` — no new endpoint needed, `/api/metrics` already returns `computed_at`.

Two decisions actually fork it:
1. **Cadence vs. waste** — a naive fixed interval works, but most polls will return byte-identical rows between minute boundaries. Better: poll, but skip re-rendering unless the returned `computed_at` differs from the last-seen value.
2. **Idle tabs** — pause the interval via the Page Visibility API when the tab isn't focused, so backgrounded dashboards don't keep invoking the function forever.

Left out: retry/backoff on fetch failure, and staggering each client's poll offset so they're not all hitting the endpoint in the same instant right after the minute rolls over — worth adding if viewer count grows, not before.

The core fix is idempotency, not just "try again": tag each charge attempt with an idempotency key before sending it to the processor, so a timeout can be retried with the same key without risking a double charge. Retry only on timeout/network errors (5xx, socket timeout) — a real decline is not retryable and should surface the actual decline reason, not a generic "payment failed".

The fork that actually matters is synchronous vs. async retry. Inline retry (1-2 attempts with short backoff before responding to the customer) is simpler but still shows "failed" for anything that takes longer than the request timeout. The more robust version returns a "processing" state immediately, retries in a background job with exponential backoff up to N attempts, and reconciles by polling the processor's charge status (using the idempotency key) rather than assuming timeout = failure — then webhooks/notifies the customer with the real final outcome. Given charges timing out multiple times a day, the async version is worth the extra plumbing since it also fixes the "customer sees failed but was actually charged" risk, not just the UX.

Index each product's name and description into a Postgres `tsvector` column (name weighted higher via `setweight`) with a GIN index, and query with `plainto_tsquery`/`websearch_to_tsquery` ranked by `ts_rank` — that's the whole build if you're already on Postgres and don't need much beyond word-match relevance.

Two forks decide if that's enough: if you need typo tolerance or fast as-you-type results, or the catalog runs into the millions of rows / high query volume, move to a dedicated engine (Meilisearch or Typesense for low ops, OpenSearch/Elasticsearch if you already run one) since Postgres FTS won't do fuzzy matching well. Separately, decide how the index stays fresh — a trigger updating the `tsvector` in the same write transaction is simplest; a dedicated search engine instead needs a sync path (dual-write or CDC) for product updates.

Left out: query autocomplete/typeahead UI, synonym handling, and personalized ranking — those are follow-ups once basic relevance ships.

Recommended approach: the client resizes/compresses each photo (cap the long edge around 1600–2000px, convert HEIC to JPEG/WebP at ~80% quality) before upload, then uploads directly to object storage via a short-lived presigned URL; the app server just creates a listing-photo row with the storage key once the upload completes. A background job or on-demand image transform (Cloudflare Images, imgproxy, etc.) derives thumbnail/detail variants afterward.

Two decisions actually fork this:
- Client-side vs. server-side resize: client-side keeps uploads fast over cellular (a 10MB phone HEIC shrinks to ~300KB before it leaves the device) but means shipping decode/resize/HEIC-conversion logic to the client; server-side is simpler code but sends full-size originals over often-poor mobile links.
- Direct-to-storage (presigned URL) vs. proxying uploads through your app server: direct-to-storage scales without loading server memory/bandwidth per photo and is the standard pattern; proxying is easier to bolt validation onto but makes your server the bottleneck for every photo.

I'd default to client-side resize + direct-to-storage. The next level down is per-photo upload retry/state (since mobile networks drop mid-upload) and the variant-generation pipeline — worth designing once this shape is agreed on.

The CDN is already the caching layer here — it just isn't allowed to work. `middleware/security.js:8` sets `no-store` on every response app-wide, applied to `/p` along with `/account` because that was the fastest way to close the 2024 audit finding (`app.js:9`). Since the CDN honors whatever `Cache-Control` the origin sends, that one line is the entire cause of the 0% hit rate — fix that and most repeat requests never reach the app or the database at all.

The fork: `/account` genuinely can't be cached by anything in front of the app (`routes/account.js:6`) — leave that as `no-store, private`. `/p` is anonymous and identical for every user (`routes/products.js:6`), so scope the security middleware to `/account` only, and give `/p` its own header — something like `public, max-age=60, stale-while-revalidate=300`. Catalog data and `relatedProducts` (the 600ms join) change a few times a day, so they tolerate a real TTL fine.

The one thing that doesn't fit that TTL cleanly is `stockFor` — it's the most volatile of the three queries and caching it at page level for a minute risks showing stale stock. If that staleness is acceptable for display purposes, cache the whole page together and stop there. If not, split it out: cache `productBySlug` + `relatedProducts` at the page level (that's ~640ms of the 900ms gone on a hit), and serve stock from an uncached or very-short-TTL fragment/endpoint so it stays near-real-time without dragging the rest of the page's cache lifetime down with it.

The auth middleware in `routes/api.js:9-19` already resolves `req.client.client_id` per request — that's the key to limit on, not IP, since the comment notes one client uses many addresses and multiple clients share a NAT. Do the check right there, before the DB query, since that's what's actually getting hammered.

State has to live in Redis. `app.js` runs 4 clustered workers per box with nothing shared in-process, and `redis.js` already shows Redis as the one piece of state every worker/box has in common — an in-memory counter per worker would undercount by 4x+ and let a client burst past the limit by hitting different workers.

Use a token-bucket (or sliding-window counter) done as a single Redis Lua script (`EVAL`), not a separate `GET` then `SET` — two round-trips race across concurrent workers and let a burst slip through between the check and the increment. Key as `ratelimit:{client_id}`, values driven by `req.client.plan` so limits are tunable per plan rather than hardcoded. On rejection, return `429` with `Retry-After` and `X-RateLimit-Remaining` headers so the client can back off instead of retrying blind.

Left out: what the actual per-plan numbers should be, and whether to rate-limit writes (`POST /reports`) more strictly than reads — that's a product call, not an architecture one.

Given the constraints in `PLATFORM.md`: no WebSockets (edge returns 501 on any upgrade), no SSE/long-lived connections (instances freeze between invocations, functions die at 10s anyway), and no shared state across instances to push from — polling is the only option, not a choice.

The other fork is interval. `rollup.md` says the table only changes once a minute, on the minute, so polling faster than that just adds load for no new data. Poll every 15–20s (cheap insurance against clock skew between your poller and the job) rather than on some short "live" cadence.

Concretely: in `public/dashboard.js`, replace the click-only wiring with `setInterval(load, 15000)` alongside the existing listeners — `load()` and the `no-store` header are already correct, so no server changes needed.

Left out: pausing the interval via the Page Visibility API when the tab isn't focused, to avoid every idle browser tab polling forever.

The fork is idempotency, not the retry loop itself: a timeout doesn't tell you whether the charge landed on the processor's side, so a naive retry risks double-charging the customer.

**Recommended shape:**
- Generate one idempotency key per logical charge attempt (e.g. tied to the cart/order ID), and send that same key on every retry. Stripe/Adyen/etc. use it to return the original result instead of creating a second charge.
- On timeout, don't immediately show "payment failed" — that's a false negative, since the charge may have succeeded. Retry a couple of times with short backoff before responding; if still unresolved, mark the order "processing" and let a webhook/async reconciliation job confirm success or failure.

**The two decisions that actually fork the design:**
1. **Sync vs. async retry** — a couple of quick inline retries (simple, but holds the request open) vs. queue a background job and return "processing" immediately (better UX for slow processors, needs a status-polling or webhook path on the frontend).
2. **Where the idempotency key lives** — generated client-side per checkout attempt vs. server-side per order row — determines whether a page refresh/resubmit during a timeout also stays safe.

Left out: backoff/retry-count tuning, and how reconciliation reruns for charges the processor never acknowledged at all (not just timeouts).

Depends on catalog size and how much relevance/typo-tolerance you need — that's the fork:

- **Small-to-medium catalog (up to ~100k products), low query volume**: Postgres full-text search (`tsvector` column over name+description, GIN index) or `pg_trgm` for fuzzy/substring matching. No new infrastructure, ranks decently with `ts_rank`.
- **Larger catalog, high query volume, or you want typo-tolerance/autocomplete/faceting**: a dedicated search engine (Elasticsearch/OpenSearch self-hosted, or Typesense/Meilisearch/Algolia hosted) with an indexing pipeline that syncs from the product DB on write.

Recommendation: start with Postgres FTS unless you already know volume or relevance demands will outgrow it — it's the cheapest to ship and migrating to a dedicated engine later is a contained change if search stays behind one API.

Left out: keeping the index in sync with product edits (sync job vs. dual-write), and relevance tuning (field weighting, ranking by popularity/recency).

Direct-to-S3 upload, bypassing the app server entirely for the bytes: the client asks the app for a signed PUT URL (`storage.signedUrl(key, {method: 'PUT'})` — already implemented but unused), uploads the photo straight to the bucket with that URL, then calls back to the app to record the key (`db.addPhotoKey`).

The fork that matters here: don't proxy the image bytes through nginx/the app. That listener's `client_max_body_size 1m` is fixed for PCI reasons tied to the payments service on the same listener, and per-location overrides were already declined — a phone photo is routinely 3-10MB, so a proxied-upload path would just fail at the edge. Signed PUT sidesteps it, and the bucket's CORS is already opened for `market.example.com` PUT.

Left out: multi-photo ordering, validation/thumbnailing, and whether to compress client-side before the PUT.

Cache the DB reads, not the HTTP response: put a read-through cache (Redis) in front of the product-fetch queries, keyed by product ID (+ variant), with invalidation triggered on write (product update/price/stock change) rather than relying on TTL alone — TTL becomes just a safety net (a few minutes) for missed invalidations.

The one thing that forks this: is the page personalized (price tiers, inventory-per-warehouse, logged-in pricing, cart state)? If no, you can go further and cache full rendered HTML/JSON at a CDN or edge layer, which kills the 900ms entirely for cache hits. If yes, you cache the expensive shared parts (product data, reviews, related items) server-side and still render per-request, so gains are smaller but personalization stays correct.

Depth I'm leaving out: cache stampede protection (lock/single-flight on miss) and warming strategy for new/hot products — worth designing once you pick which of the two paths above fits your page.

Two things already in the code shape this more than anything else:

- **Key by `client_id`, not IP.** The auth middleware in `routes/api.js:6-8` already notes clients share IPs behind corporate NAT and one client can call from many IPs — IP-based limiting would both block innocent bystanders and fail to catch the offender. Key off `req.client.client_id`, which is already resolved before your route handlers run.
- **Counter storage has to be Redis, not in-process.** `app.js` forks 4 workers per box with nothing shared in module scope, and there's a fleet of boxes behind the LB — an in-memory counter would undercount by 4x per box and reset per box. `redis.js` already gives you a shared client every worker can hit, so put the counter there.

Concretely: a middleware in `routes/api.js` right after the key-auth check, keyed on `req.client.client_id`, checking a limit from `req.client.plan` (the row already carries plan). Use an atomic Redis op — `INCR` + `PEXPIRE` for a simple fixed window, or a Lua script over a sorted set if you want a sliding window that doesn't let a client burst 2x at the window boundary. Reject with `429` and a `Retry-After` header before the DB query runs, so the offending client's load never reaches Postgres either.

That's the shape; the remaining depth is picking fixed-window vs. sliding-window and the actual per-plan numbers, which is a tuning question, not an architecture one.

Push updates from the server rather than having the client poll: have the backend emit an event whenever the underlying data changes, and keep an SSE (or WebSocket) connection open from the dashboard that applies incremental patches to the UI as events arrive.

The fork that matters is SSE vs. WebSocket vs. polling. SSE is the right default for a one-directional "server tells me things changed" dashboard — simpler than WebSockets, works over plain HTTP, auto-reconnects. WebSockets only earn their complexity if the dashboard also needs to send data back (e.g., acking an alert) in real time. Plain short-interval polling is the fallback if you can't run a long-lived connection at all (e.g., behind infra that kills idle connections).

The second fork is single-instance vs. multi-instance backend. If the app runs on more than one server process, you need a pub/sub layer (Redis, NATS, etc.) so an event published from one instance reaches clients connected to another — a single in-process event emitter won't do it.

Left out at this level: how you detect the underlying change (DB triggers, outbox pattern, or the write path just publishing after it commits) and reconnection/backfill logic for a client that was offline. What's the dashboard's backend stack?

The bug isn't retry logic — it's that a client-side timeout gets treated as a failure when the charge may have actually gone through on the processor's side. Fix that conflation first, then add retries.

**Core mechanism: idempotency key + reconciliation, not blind retry**
Every charge attempt sends an idempotency key (one per logical purchase, generated client- or server-side before the first attempt). On a timeout, don't assume failure and don't just fire the request again — look up the charge by that key first. Most processors (Stripe, Braintree, etc.) will either return the original result or safely no-op a duplicate request with the same key. Retrying without this risks double-charging when the original request actually succeeded but the response never made it back.

**The fork that matters: classify the error before deciding whether to retry**
- Timeout / network error / 5xx from the processor: outcome unknown, safe to reconcile-then-retry.
- Card decline / insufficient funds / fraud block: outcome known, retrying won't help — show the real reason, don't retry.
Conflating these two is usually what produces the generic "payment failed" message today.

**Where retries live:** move this off the synchronous request path into a background job (queue with backoff + jitter, capped attempts, e.g. 3 tries over a couple minutes). The customer's browser already gave up waiting; retrying inline just times them out again. Show "processing" instead of "payment failed" for the timeout case, then push the real outcome via webhook or a status poll.

Left out: specific backoff intervals, queue/worker choice, and webhook signature verification — those are implementation details once the idempotency-key + classification split is in place.

Recommendation: start with Postgres full-text search — a generated `tsvector` column combining name (weighted A) and description (weighted B), a GIN index on it, and `ts_rank` for ordering results. That handles "type a few words, get matches by name/description" with no new infrastructure, assuming the catalog already lives in Postgres.

Two things fork this:
- **Catalog size / latency needs**: fine into the low hundreds of thousands of products; past that, or if you need fuzzy/typo-tolerant matching and faceted filtering at consistent low latency, move to a dedicated search engine (Typesense or Meilisearch are simplest to run; Elasticsearch/OpenSearch if you need more).
- **Match quality expectations**: if "search" should also catch conceptual matches (query "sofa" finding a product described as "couch"), that needs embeddings + vector search layered on top — full-text alone won't do it.

Left out: the pipeline that keeps the search index in sync as products are added/edited (trigger-based for Postgres, or a reindex job for an external engine) — that's the next thing to design once the storage choice is picked.

Two decisions actually fork this:

**Upload path**: presigned URL direct-to-object-storage (S3/GCS) rather than proxying bytes through your API server. Phone camera photos run 3–12MB each; routing that through your app server just to relay it to storage burns memory/bandwidth and risks timeouts on cellular connections for no benefit — the server only needs to hand out a short-lived signed URL and record the resulting object key once the client confirms.

**Where resizing happens**: client-side downscale/compress before upload (canvas or native resize to something like a 2000px-longest-edge JPEG) versus uploading full-size and doing it server-side. On cellular, shrinking client-side cuts upload time and data usage significantly; the tradeoff is you lose the original for later use (e.g. if you ever want print-quality). Most listing apps take the size/speed win and treat the upload as final.

Depth I'm leaving out: the async thumbnail pipeline (a worker producing display/thumb sizes off the original), EXIF orientation correction, and resumable/retry behavior for uploads that drop mid-transfer on a bad connection — worth designing once the above two are settled.

Cache-aside with Redis, keyed by product ID (plus locale/currency/variant if the page differs by those), storing the data needed to render the page rather than final HTML — cheap to invalidate, still skips the DB read. Back it with a short TTL (a few minutes) as a safety net, and add request-coalescing around cache misses (single-flight per key) so a popular product's expiry doesn't send a burst of concurrent requests straight to the DB.

The real fork is invalidation: TTL-only is simpler but leaves a staleness window after edits; event-driven (bust the key on product/price update) is fresher but requires the write path to know which keys to clear. Given the DB is the bottleneck and product pages are presumably read-heavy, go with write-path invalidation as primary and TTL as backstop.

Two things from the code settle most of the design:

- `app.js` forks 4 worker processes per box with nothing shared except Redis (`redis.js`'s own comment says as much) — so any counter has to live in Redis, not process memory, or you'd undercount per-box by ~4x and reset on every restart/deploy.
- `routes/api.js` already resolves `req.client` (`client_id`, `plan`) from the API key before your route handlers run, and its comment explicitly warns IP is a bad key — NAT'd clients share addresses. So limit by `client_id`, not IP.

Concretely: add a middleware in `routes/api.js` right after the API-key auth block (it needs `req.client`), before the route handlers, so an over-limit request gets rejected before it ever reaches `db.query`. Track usage in Redis under a key like `ratelimit:{client_id}`, with the limit pulled from `req.client.plan` since that's already fetched.

The one real fork: fixed-window counter (`INCR` + `PEXPIRE`) vs. a token bucket done as a Lua script. Fixed-window is two round trips and lets a client burst up to 2x right at the window boundary — the exact "hammering" pattern you're trying to stop. A token bucket in a single Lua script is atomic and smooths that out, at the cost of a slightly more involved script. I'd pick the Lua token bucket here given the symptom is bursty abuse, not steady overuse.

Left out at this depth: the actual Lua script, response headers (`Retry-After`/`X-RateLimit-*`), and whether to also cap at the LB/box level as a second line of defense.

Recommendation: server-sent events (SSE) pushed from the backend, not client polling — one-way updates fit "dashboard reflects state," and SSE is plain HTTP (no WebSocket infra) with built-in reconnect.

Two decisions actually fork the design:

1. **How the backend learns data changed.** Either it already has a natural event (a job queue, DB trigger, message bus) it can hook to push immediately, or it doesn't and you're stuck re-querying on an interval (e.g. every 5s) and diffing before emitting. The former gives real-time updates for free; the latter caps freshness at your poll interval and adds query load per connected client.
2. **Fan-out to many open dashboard tabs.** One SSE connection per browser tab hitting your app server works fine at low viewer counts; past a few dozen concurrent viewers you want a pub/sub layer (Redis, etc.) between "thing changed" and "push to N connections" so you're not re-running the source query per client.

Left out: auth/reconnect-token handling for SSE, and the fallback path (polling) for proxies that buffer SSE badly.

Recommendation: retry only on timeout/connection errors (never on a 4xx from the vendor — that's a real decline), and always send the same `Idempotency-Key` on every attempt for a given order. Per PROVIDER.md, a timeout means "unknown, not failed," and the vendor already dedupes by key — so a retry after a timeout either gets the original charge back or completes it, and never double-charges.

The two decisions that actually fork the design:

1. **Where the key comes from.** It has to be generated and persisted (e.g. `orders.charge_attempt_key`) *before* the first `charge()` call, not inside the retry loop — otherwise a process crash between "timeout" and "retry" loses the key and a fresh attempt on restart charges the customer twice. Something like `charge_attempt_key = orders:{id}:{n}` written in the same transaction that reads the order works.
2. **Bounded retry with backoff around `payments.charge`** in `payments.js` itself (not in the route handler), catching only the timeout/`ECONNRESET`-style errors and re-throwing anything with a `statusCode`. `routes/checkout.js:28-32` currently treats every rejection as "payment failed" — that catch block needs to distinguish exhausted-retries-on-unknown-status (show the customer "we're confirming your payment," reconcile async) from a genuine decline (show "payment failed" as it does now).

Left out: backoff timing/jitter values, and what happens if all retries exhaust while the true state is still unknown (needs a reconciliation job that queries the vendor by idempotency key, since you can't just mark it failed).

Use Postgres full-text search (`tsvector` over name + description, GIN index) if the catalog is small-to-mid sized and already lives in Postgres — no new infra, and it handles ranking and partial-word matches out of the box. Move to a dedicated engine (OpenSearch/Elasticsearch/Meilisearch) only once you need typo-tolerance, faceting, or the catalog grows large enough that DB-side search starts costing query latency.

Two forks that actually change the design:
- **Keyword vs semantic search** — a few words against name/description is squarely keyword-search territory (BM25-style ranking), not embeddings; only reach for vector/semantic search if you expect vague or descriptive queries that don't share vocabulary with the product text.
- **Freshness** — if products update frequently, decide between synchronous index updates (simple, can add write latency) versus an async pipeline (queue + indexer) that trades a short staleness window for decoupling.

Left out: relevance tuning (field weighting, synonyms), autocomplete/typeahead as a separate concern from search, and pagination/caching — worth a follow-up once the base engine choice is made.

Direct-to-storage upload: client requests a presigned URL from your API, uploads the file straight to S3/GCS/R2, then confirms with the API to attach it to the listing. That keeps multi-megabyte camera photos off your app servers and lets uploads run in parallel per photo.

The fork worth deciding: resize/compress client-side before upload (canvas or `createImageBitmap`, downscale to ~2000px, re-encode as JPEG/WebP) versus uploading raw and processing server-side. Client-side compression cuts upload time and mobile data usage dramatically — a 12MP camera photo is often 5–10MB uncompressed — but you still need a server-side (or queued/Lambda-style) step afterward to generate thumbnail/detail variants and strip EXIF/GPS metadata for privacy, since you can't trust the client for that. Do both: compress client-side for upload speed, then reprocess server-side for the variants you actually serve.

Everything else — retry/resumable upload for flaky mobile connections, ordering/cover-photo selection, per-listing photo limits — is a smaller layer on top of that.

Cache-aside in Redis (or similar), keyed by product ID, storing the assembled page data rather than raw query rows, with a short TTL as a backstop plus explicit invalidation fired on product-update events.

The fork that matters: TTL-only vs event-driven invalidation. TTL-only is simpler but leaves a staleness window (price/inventory can lag); event-driven is fresher but needs a reliable hook into wherever products get written, so it works well when updates funnel through one path (e.g., an admin service) and gets messy if they come from several. Given DB load is the actual pain point here, event-driven is the better fit unless product writes are scattered across many code paths.

Left out: stampede protection when a hot key expires (locking or jittered TTLs), and whether to also cache at the edge/CDN for anonymous traffic.

Key it on `req.client.client_id`, which the existing auth middleware in `routes/api.js` already resolves before your handlers run — not on IP, since your own comment notes clients share NATs and span multiple addresses, so IP would both overblock innocent co-tenants and underblock the abusive client.

Enforce it in Redis, not in-process memory. `redis.js` shows you already run one Redis shared across every worker and every box; `app.js` clusters 4 workers per box with separate heaps, so an in-memory counter would only ever see a quarter of one box's traffic and miss the rest entirely. Add a small Lua script that does the increment-and-check atomically against a key like `rl:{client_id}:{window}`, so concurrent requests across workers don't race.

One real fork: fixed-window `INCR`+`EXPIRE` is one line and cheap, but lets a client burst up to 2x the limit across a window boundary. A token-bucket (still one atomic Lua call) avoids that at the cost of a few more lines. Given this is the client already causing pain, go with token bucket — the whole point is smoothing bursts, not just capping totals.

Wire it as middleware in `routes/api.js` right after the auth check (so `req.client` is populated), pulling the limit from `req.client.plan`; on exceed, return 429 with `Retry-After`.

Left out: what happens when Redis itself is slow or unreachable — fail-open (let traffic through, risk the same problem) vs fail-closed (block everyone, risk an outage from a dependency blip). That's a deliberate call, not a default.

Two forks decide the design:

**Push vs. poll.** Polling (dashboard re-fetches every N seconds) is simplest to build and fine if near-real-time (5-30s lag) is acceptable. Push (WebSocket or Server-Sent Events) is needed if updates must appear within a second or two, but costs more: you need a connection-holding server, reconnect/backoff logic on the client, and a way to fan out server-side events to connected clients.

**Where the "something changed" signal comes from.** Either the dashboard backend re-queries its data source on a timer and diffs/pushes what changed, or the underlying systems (DB, job queue, metrics store) emit events that flow directly into the dashboard's push layer. The former is easy to bolt onto an existing dashboard; the latter is more real-time but requires hooking into each data source's change mechanism (DB triggers/CDC, pub/sub, webhooks).

Recommendation: start with SSE + server-side polling of the existing data source every few seconds — it's a one-way stream (simpler than WebSocket since the dashboard only receives, never sends), works over plain HTTP, and reconnects natively in browsers. Upgrade to event-driven push only if the underlying systems already emit change events and sub-second latency matters.

The core problem: a timeout means you don't know whether the charge actually landed on the processor's side, so a naive retry risks double-charging. That makes this a reconciliation problem first, retry-loop second.

**Recommended shape:**
1. Generate one idempotency key per checkout attempt (not per HTTP call) and reuse it on every retry of that same charge — Stripe/Braintree/Adyen etc. all support this natively and will return the original result instead of charging twice.
2. On timeout, don't show "failed" — show "processing" and hand off to a background job instead of retrying inline. Inline retry just stacks more latency onto a call that already timed out.
3. That job first checks the charge's actual status via the processor's API (or waits for the webhook) before doing anything — the charge may well have succeeded despite the timeout.
4. Only if still unresolved does it retry with the same idempotency key, with a few bounded attempts and exponential backoff.
5. If it's still unresolved after that window, surface a real failure with a support/contact path — don't leave the user on "processing" forever.

**The one decision that actually forks this:** whether you trust the idempotency key alone to make blind retries safe, or you require a status check/webhook confirmation before every retry. The key alone is usually enough if your processor's idempotency guarantee is solid; add the explicit status check if you've been burned by edge cases (network blips between you and the processor where the key wasn't even received) or need faster user-facing resolution than waiting on retries.

What's your payment processor? That determines whether idempotency keys are a built-in primitive or something you'd need to implement yourself.

Client side: resize/compress in-browser (canvas or `createImageBitmap`) before upload — phone photos run 3-8MB at 4000px+, and sellers will be on patchy mobile connections, so shrinking to ~1600px/JPEG-80 client-side cuts upload time and server load a lot.

Transfer: direct-to-storage via presigned URL (S3/GCS/R2), not through your app server — request a presigned PUT from your backend, upload straight from the browser, then notify the backend to attach the resulting key to the listing. Avoids streaming binary through your API process.

Server side: on upload-complete webhook/callback, generate thumbnail + display sizes (Lambda/Cloud Function or a job queue), validate it's actually an image (magic-byte check, not just extension), and strip EXIF (GPS tags in phone photos are a real privacy leak for sellers).

Listing model: store an ordered list of photo references on the listing, with one job handling reordering/primary-photo selection and deletion of orphaned uploads (sellers abandon uploads mid-flow often).

Fork: background-job image processing (thumbnails, EXIF strip) vs. doing it synchronously in the presigned-upload callback — background is the right call once you have any retry/scale need, synchronous is fine if this is a weekend-project MVP. Which one matches where this app is?

Cache at the edge, not in the app. `/p/:slug` is genuinely anonymous — no session read, price/stock/copy identical for everyone — and the CDN already sits in front of every request, honoring whatever `Cache-Control` the origin sends. It shows 0% hit rate today only because `security.js` slaps `no-store, no-cache, private` on *every* route, `/p` included. That blanket policy was the fast fix for the 2024 finding (an `/account` page leaking to the wrong user via an intermediary cache) and was never scoped back down. Fixing that scope is the actual lever: a CDN hit skips the app and the DB entirely, beating any Redis-in-front-of-Postgres scheme on latency.

Two things fork the design from there:

1. **Where the no-store boundary lives.** Don't touch the app-wide default in `security.js` — that's what's correctly protecting `/account` (still per-user, still must never be cached by anything in front). Add a route-level override in `routes/products.js` that sets its own `Cache-Control: public, max-age=...` for `/p`, since catalog edits land a few times a day, not per-request.

2. **Stock doesn't share the catalog's TTL.** `stockFor` is inventory-derived and plausibly moves faster than product copy (orders draining it between admin edits). Caching it at the same multi-minute TTL as `productBySlug`/`relatedProducts` risks showing "in stock" after a sellout. Either pull it out of the cached page fragment and query it live (it's the cheap one at ~250ms vs. `relatedProducts`' ~600ms), or give it its own short-TTL cache key separate from the page cache.

Rate-limit at the edge (API gateway or a shared middleware in front of `/v1`), keyed on client identity, using a token-bucket counter backed by a shared store like Redis (atomic `INCR`+`EXPIRE` or a Lua script) so the count holds across all app instances, not just one. Reject over-limit requests with `429` and a `Retry-After` header.

Two things actually fork the design:

1. **Client identification** — if requests carry an API key/auth token, key the bucket on that (what you want, since you already know which client is hammering it). Falling back to IP is coarser and trivially works around via multiple IPs/NAT.
2. **Where the counter lives** — in-memory per-instance counters are cheap but let a client stay under the limit on each instance while blowing past it in aggregate; a shared Redis counter fixes that at the cost of a network round-trip per request.

Left out: burst/refill tuning, per-plan tiered limits, and choice of algorithm variant (token bucket vs. sliding-window log) — worth a follow-up once the above is in place.

Push the data instead of having the client poll for it: have the server emit updates over Server-Sent Events (or a WebSocket if you need bidirectional traffic) whenever the underlying metrics change, and have the dashboard just re-render on each message. SSE is the simpler choice for a read-only dashboard — plain HTTP, auto-reconnect built in — while WebSockets only earn their complexity if the dashboard needs to send anything back (filters, acks, etc.).

What's the dashboard's stack (frontend framework, backend language, and where the ops data currently lives — DB polling loop, message queue, existing metrics store)? That decides whether "push on change" means hooking into an existing event stream or wrapping a periodic query in a broadcast.

Two things in `PROVIDER.md` decide the shape of this: a timeout is explicitly **unknown, not failed**, and the vendor supports `Idempotency-Key` but `payments.js` never sends one. Naive retry-on-timeout without that key double-charges the customer, so the key is the mechanism that makes retrying safe at all.

**Core change:** generate a stable idempotency key per order (order id works, since one order should ever produce one successful charge) and send it on every attempt for that order, including retries. Store it on the order row before the first attempt so a retry — inline or later — reuses it and collapses to the original charge instead of authorizing twice.

**The fork:** where the retry loop lives.
- Inline in `checkout.js`'s handler — retry the timeout a couple of times with backoff before giving up. Simple, no new infra, but a process crash mid-attempt still leaves the order stuck, and the customer waits longer per request.
- Async reconciliation — on timeout, mark the order `payment_unknown` (not `failed`) and return that to the customer instead of a hard failure; a background job retries or looks up the charge by the idempotency key later.

Pick inline retry (2-3 attempts, backoff) for the common case you described — a few timeouts a day are almost certainly transient — but keep the `payment_unknown` status and a reconciliation sweep as the fallback for when inline retries also time out or the process dies mid-request. You need the sweep regardless, since idempotency alone doesn't cover a crash between the vendor accepting the charge and your process recording it.

Left for the next level: backoff/attempt counts, and the reconciliation job's polling cadence and lookup call (`GET` by idempotency key vs. by charge id, per whatever Cardstream exposes beyond what's summarized here).

For a catalog in the tens-to-low-hundreds-of-thousands of products, start with Postgres full-text search: a generated `tsvector` column combining name (weighted higher) and description, a GIN index, results ranked by `ts_rank`. No new service, and it's usually fast enough.

Two things fork this:
- **Catalog size / query volume** — past roughly a few hundred thousand products or heavy query load, move to a dedicated engine (Meilisearch or Typesense for low ops overhead, Elasticsearch/OpenSearch if you need more control over relevance).
- **Typo tolerance** — Postgres FTS won't forgive misspellings. If that matters, add `pg_trgm` similarity on top, or skip straight to a dedicated engine, which handles fuzzy matching natively.

What's the current stack and roughly how many products? That decides which path applies. Left out of scope here: relevance tuning, keeping the search index in sync as products are edited, and autocomplete/typeahead.

Direct-to-storage upload with client-side compression first, since phone photos run 5–50MB and you don't want to hold connections open proxying that through your app server or store them uncompressed.

Flow: client requests a presigned upload URL from your API (which just writes a pending row: listing_id, seller, status), client resizes/compresses the image in-browser (canvas or an image library) to something like max 2000px/reasonable JPEG quality, uploads straight to S3/GCS with that URL, then confirms completion to your API which flips the row to active and kicks off async thumbnail generation.

The one thing that'll bite you if skipped: strip EXIF GPS data server-side (or on upload) before the photo is public — phone photos embed exact location by default, and a marketplace listing is exactly the context where you don't want a seller's home address leaking.

Cache-aside in Redis, keyed by product ID, populated on read-miss from the DB query that's costing you the 900ms — that alone should take most pages to single-digit ms. Invalidate explicitly on product writes (update/price/stock change) rather than relying on TTL alone, with a short TTL (minutes) as a backstop for missed invalidations.

The one real fork: are these pages the same for every visitor (no per-user pricing/inventory/personalization)? If yes, put a CDN/edge cache in front too and this becomes mostly a solved problem — cache-aside in Redis is just the origin fallback. If pages vary per user, you're stuck at the app-cache layer, and the depth you'd need to get into next is what's cacheable per-request vs per-product (e.g. cache the product data, compute personalization separately).

Enforce it in `routes/api.js`, right after the key lookup resolves `req.client` — key the limiter by `client_id`, not IP. The comment in that file already flags why: clients share NAT addresses, so IP-based limiting would throttle the wrong tenants.

Use the existing Redis client (`redis.js`) — it's already the one thing shared across all 4 workers × all boxes, same as sessions. A Lua script doing an atomic token-bucket check (`rl:{client_id}`, refill rate from `req.client.plan`) is the right primitive: one round trip, no race between workers, and it absorbs bursts instead of hard-cutting at a window boundary the way a plain `INCR`+`EXPIRE` fixed window would. On exceed, `429` with `Retry-After` before the request touches Postgres — that's the actual goal, since it's `db.query` load degrading things for everyone.

The one thing this doesn't cover: limits are per-key, so a client rotating across multiple API keys evades it — worth deciding now whether that's in scope or a later problem.

The fork is push vs. poll. Short polling (client re-fetches every N seconds) is the simplest to build and is fine if the data doesn't need to feel instant — a few lines of `setInterval` plus a fetch, no backend changes if an API already exists. Server-sent events (SSE) push updates the moment data changes and are still simple (plain HTTP, auto-reconnect built into `EventSource`), but need the backend to notify on writes rather than just serve reads. WebSockets only earn their complexity if the dashboard needs to send data back too.

For an ops dashboard specifically, I'd pick SSE: it's one-directional, deals fine with proxies/load balancers, and avoids hammering the server with polling load while still being far simpler than WebSockets. The second decision is where the "changed" signal comes from — either the backend emits an event whenever the underlying data mutates, or a lightweight watcher polls the data source and diffs it before pushing to clients. Which one fits depends on whether the ops data lives in something you control the write-path for (emit directly) or an external system (need the watcher).

Read `payments.js`, `routes/checkout.js`, and `PROVIDER.md`. The vendor doc is the crux: a timeout on `/v2/charges` means **unknown**, not failed — the charge may have gone through. `checkout.js` currently maps every exception, including a timeout, straight to `502 payment failed`, and `payments.js` never sends the `Idempotency-Key` header the vendor supports.

Recommendation: generate an idempotency key once per order (persist it on the order row when it's created, or on first payment attempt), pass it on every call to `charge()` including retries, and retry only on timeout with a couple of bounded attempts and backoff — a 4xx from the provider is a real decline, not something to retry. If retries are exhausted, don't write `status = 'failed'`; write something like `payment_pending`/`unknown` and reconcile out of band, since the vendor is explicit that "no response" isn't "no charge."

The two decisions that actually fork this:
- **Where the key lives.** Generated fresh per HTTP request breaks idempotency the moment you retry (each attempt authorises separately); it has to be stored against the order and reused across every attempt for that order.
- **What "exhausted retries" means to the customer.** Falling back to today's `payment failed` is simplest but is exactly the wrong answer per the vendor doc — it can double-charge on a subsequent manual retry from the customer. Surfacing pending/unknown and resolving asynchronously is correct but means checkout can no longer promise a synchronous paid/failed answer.

Left out: exact backoff/attempt-count tuning, and how the pending case gets resolved (webhook from the provider vs. a polling job that re-queries the charge by idempotency key).

Depends on your current datastore. If products already live in Postgres/MySQL, add a `tsvector`/`FULLTEXT` column over name + description with a GIN/FULLTEXT index and rank by `ts_rank` — no new infra, good enough for exact/stemmed keyword matches. If you need typo-tolerance, instant-as-you-type results, or better relevance out of the box, put a dedicated search engine (Typesense or Meilisearch, self-hosted; Algolia if you'd rather not run it) in front, synced from the product table via a change feed or nightly reindex.

The one fork that matters: keyword search (above) assumes users type words that appear in the product text. If the requirement is closer to "find me a warm jacket" matching a product titled "insulated parka," that's semantic search (embeddings + vector index), a different build entirely. Worth confirming which one "product search" means before scoping further.

Direct-to-storage: client requests a presigned upload URL from the backend, uploads the photo straight to S3/GCS/R2, then pings the backend to attach it to the listing. Keeps large phone photos (often 5–15MB HEIC/JPEG) off your app servers instead of proxying bytes through them.

Two decisions actually fork this:

- **Where resizing happens.** Client-side downscale (canvas/createImageBitmap, cap to ~2048px, re-encode JPEG) before upload cuts upload time on cellular and storage cost, but server-side thumbnailing via a queued worker is what you rely on for correctness across devices/browsers — do the client resize as an optimization, not as your only pass.
- **How the record gets confirmed.** Either the client calls back to the backend after a successful PUT, or you use the storage provider's completion webhook/event notification. The callback is simpler; the webhook is more reliable if the client drops mid-flow (backgrounded app, lost connection) since the record won't otherwise become "attached."

Everything else — EXIF stripping, moderation scan, multiple-photos-per-listing ordering — is standard plumbing once those two are picked.

Recommendation: cache at the data layer, not the page layer — put a read-through cache (Redis) in front of the product query itself, keyed by `product_id` (+ variant/locale if those change the query). Since the DB is nearly all of the 900ms, this captures almost the whole win without touching rendering.

Two decisions that actually fork the design:

1. **Invalidation strategy** — TTL-only (simple, but stale price/stock for up to N seconds) vs event-driven (product writes publish an invalidation for that key). For price/inventory, use event-driven invalidation with a short TTL as a backstop for the events you miss.
2. **Stampede protection** — a cold or just-invalidated key still costs 900ms; if the page gets concurrent traffic, uncoordinated misses will all hit the DB at once. Use request coalescing (single-flight per key) or serve-stale-while-revalidate so only one request refills the cache.

Left out: which tier to use (Redis vs in-process vs CDN/edge caching for fully anonymous views) and whether to cache the raw query result vs the whole rendered fragment — that depends on how much of the page is personalized versus shared across users.

Since workers don't share memory (`app.js`'s cluster comment) and clients can't be trusted by IP (they sit behind shared NAT, per `routes/api.js:7-8`), the check has to run in Redis — the one piece of state already shared across every worker and box — keyed by `client_id`, not IP.

Concretely: add it as a step in the existing auth middleware (`routes/api.js:9-19`), right after `req.client` is resolved and before the DB query runs. A key like `ratelimit:{client_id}` checked/incremented atomically in Redis, returning 429 + `Retry-After` when tripped. Since `req.client.plan` is already fetched there, the limit can vary by tier for free.

Two decisions actually fork this:
- **Algorithm**: a fixed-window counter (`INCR` + `EXPIRE`) is trivial but lets a client burst right at the window boundary — exactly the "hammering" pattern you're trying to stop. A token bucket or sliding-window log (Lua script for atomicity) smooths that out at the cost of a slightly more complex Redis op.
- **Redis-down behavior**: fail-open (let requests through) or fail-closed (block everything). Redis is a single shared dependency here — a blip shouldn't take down `/v1` for every client, so fail-open is the safer default.

Left out: actual limit numbers per plan, and whether unauthenticated pre-auth traffic needs a separate coarse IP-based limiter in front of this (this scheme only kicks in once a valid key resolves to a `client_id`).

Poll — push is off the table here. `PLATFORM.md` says connection upgrades 501 at the edge and instances freeze between invocations, so WebSockets and SSE both die immediately on this platform; nothing you build can keep a connection open.

The one real decision is cadence, and `jobs/rollup.md` settles it: `rollup` only changes once a minute, on the minute, so polling faster than that just burns requests against a table that hasn't moved. Poll every 20-30s (cheap — `api/metrics.js` is 30ms/4KB), and skip the re-render when the returned `computed_at` matches what's already on screen, which `dashboard.js` already surfaces but never compares.

Left out: pausing the interval on `visibilitychange` so backgrounded tabs stop polling — a few lines, not a fork.

Two things have to happen together — a retry without the first is unsafe, and vice versa is pointless:

**1. Idempotency key, keyed to the order.** Right now `charge()` never sends `Idempotency-Key`, and per `PROVIDER.md` a timeout means the charge may have already gone through. Retrying as-is risks a double charge. Generate the key from `order.id` (e.g. `charge:${order.id}`) and send it on every attempt for that order, including the first — that's what makes a retry safe rather than reckless.

**2. Where the retry loop lives — this is the real fork:**
- **In-request retry** (inside `payments.charge`, wrapping the existing call 2-3 times with the same idempotency key on timeout/network error): simple, no schema change, resolves within the customer's HTTP request. Fits "a few times a day" — this is transient, not sustained outage.
- **Async/background retry** (mark the order `charging` instead of catching-and-failing, return a pending response, retry via a job or queue, update the order when it resolves): needed only if timeouts can outlast a request's reasonable time budget, or if you want to survive the server process dying mid-retry.

Given the failure rate described (a few times a day, presumably brief provider hiccups, not outages), I'd start with the in-request retry — it directly fixes the bug in `routes/checkout.js:28-32`, where a timeout is caught by the generic `catch` and shown as "payment failed" with no distinction from an actual decline. The depth I'm not covering: backoff timing/jitter, what status code and copy to show the customer if all retries are exhausted, and reconciliation (a periodic job that queries Cardstream by idempotency key for any order stuck in a pending/unknown state, in case the process dies mid-retry).

For name/description matching at typical catalog scale, start with Postgres full-text search: a `tsvector` column (name + description, weighted) with a GIN index, plus `pg_trgm` for typo tolerance on partial words. No new infrastructure if products already live in Postgres, and it's fast enough into the low millions of rows.

The fork that matters: lexical search (above) versus a dedicated engine (Typesense/Meilisearch/Elasticsearch) or embeddings. Reach for a dedicated engine only if you need faceted filtering, custom ranking, or sub-50ms latency at large scale; reach for embeddings only if users search by concept/synonym rather than words that actually appear in the text. Don't build either until lexical search proves insufficient.

Second decision, independent of the above: how the index stays in sync with catalog writes — updated transactionally in the same write path (simple, adds latency to writes) versus async via an outbox/queue (more moving parts, keeps writes fast). Pick based on how write-heavy the catalog is.

The repo already has the pieces half-assembled — reuse them rather than routing bytes through nginx.

**Why nginx is a dead end for this:** `nginx.conf:6-9` caps `client_max_body_size` at 1m globally, and raising it (or adding a per-location override) was already declined by the payments team because the limit is cited in their PCI paperwork for the shared listener. Phone camera photos routinely run 3-8MB+, so multipart uploads through `market.example.com` won't fit and re-opening that fight isn't the way in.

**What's already there for this exact purpose:** `storage.js:10-13` notes the bucket accepts signed PUT with the same credentials/helper as the existing signed-GET invoice flow, and CORS for PUT from `market.example.com` is already configured on the bucket. `db.js` already has an empty `photo_keys` array column and an `addPhotoKey(id, key)` helper waiting to be used.

**Flow:**
1. New route, e.g. `POST /:id/photos/sign` — generates a key, calls `storage.signedUrl(key, {method:'PUT'})`, returns `{key, url}`. This request/response is tiny JSON, well under the 1m cap.
2. Client PUTs the photo bytes straight to S3 with that URL — bypasses the nginx listener entirely, so the PCI-driven body limit never comes into play.
3. Client calls back, e.g. `POST /:id/photos` with the key, and the server runs `db.addPhotoKey`.

The one real fork: whether to trust that confirm callback blindly. As written, a client can claim success without uploading, or PUT arbitrary content at a guessable key — worth a server-side `HeadObject` check (and a content-type condition on the presigned PUT) before writing to `photo_keys`, rather than trusting step 3 alone.

Thumbnailing, content/virus scanning, and multi-part upload for oversized files are the next level down.

Cache the DB query results, not the whole rendered page — a read-through cache (Redis/Memcached) keyed by product ID, TTL a few minutes, sitting in front of the query layer. That collapses the 900ms mostly to cache latency on hits, and a page usually needs freshness only on a subset of its data anyway.

Two decisions actually fork this:

1. **Invalidation**: TTL-only is simplest but means stale price/stock for up to the TTL window. If price/inventory must be accurate immediately, the write path needs to publish an invalidation (or update-in-place) on product change — more moving parts, but no staleness gap.
2. **Granularity**: cache the product row/description as one long-lived entry, but keep fast-changing bits (stock count, price if it's dynamic) as separate short-TTL keys or skip caching them entirely. Lumping everything into one blob forces you to pick one staleness tolerance for data that doesn't share one.

What's the stack here (what's serving the pages, and is there already a shared cache like Redis in the loop)? That determines whether this is a drop-in read-through layer or needs new infra. Left out: cache stampede protection on expiry and cold-start warming — next level down once the above is settled.

Two decisions actually fork this, given what's here.

**Key by `client_id`, not IP.** The auth middleware in `routes/api.js:9-19` already resolves `req.client.client_id` (and `plan`) from the API key before your handlers run. The comment above it says clients share IPs behind NAT and one client uses many IPs — so an IP-keyed limiter would throttle innocent neighbors and miss the actual offender. Client ID is already sitting in `req.client`; use that as the counter key.

**Store counts in the existing Redis, not in-process memory.** `app.js` forks 4 workers per box with nothing shared between them, and `redis.js` is already the one piece of state every worker and every box has in common (used for sessions). An in-memory counter would just reset the limit 4x per box and differently per box — the offending client would sail through 3 of 4 workers. Put the limiter as middleware in `routes/api.js`, right after the key lookup, doing `INCR client:<id>:<window>` + `EXPIRE` against the shared Redis client, rejecting with 429 once the count exceeds the plan's limit.

Left out at this depth: `INCR`/`EXPIRE` isn't atomic as two round trips, so under real concurrency you'd want a small Lua script (or `redis.call` via `EVAL`) to make check-and-increment one operation, plus a decision on fail-open vs fail-closed if Redis itself is briefly unreachable.

Poll, not push. The platform rules out push entirely: `api/` functions are killed at 10s and frozen between invocations, WebSocket upgrades 501 at the edge before reaching your code, and there's no sticky routing or shared memory to hold a connection open across instances (PLATFORM.md). SSE and WebSockets are both architecturally impossible here, not just costly.

The other fork — interval length — is settled by `jobs/rollup.md`: the `rollup` table only changes once a minute, on the minute, so polling faster than that just re-fetches byte-identical rows. Poll every 20-30s (fast enough to catch the update shortly after it lands, without knowing your exact clock offset from the job) rather than trying to sync to the minute boundary.

Concretely, in `public/dashboard.js`, replace the button-only wiring with `setInterval(load, 20000)` alongside the existing click handler, and skip the re-render when `computed_at` hasn't changed from the last fetch to avoid pointless DOM churn. The next level down — backoff on fetch failure, pausing polling via the Page Visibility API when the tab is hidden — isn't needed to solve "people are hitting refresh."

Two decisions actually fork this:

**Idempotency key is load-bearing.** A timeout means you don't know if the charge landed on the processor's side — a naive retry risks double-charging. Every retry attempt must reuse the same idempotency key (tied to the order/attempt, not a fresh UUID each try) so the processor collapses duplicates into the original result.

**Retry only what's retryable, and decide sync vs async.** Timeouts/5xx/network errors are retryable; declines/insufficient-funds are not — don't retry those or you're just delaying the same "failed" message. For the retryable path, doing it inline (retry within the request before responding) is simpler but bounded by how long the customer will wait; doing it async (queue job + backoff) means introducing a "processing" order state and a way to tell the customer later (webhook/poll/email) instead of "failed" up front.

Left out: backoff schedule/max-attempt tuning, and reconciliation logic for orphaned charges (processor succeeded but your system never got the response).

Depends on what you're already running, but the two decisions that actually fork this:

**Search engine**: if products already live in Postgres, start with `tsvector` full-text search plus `pg_trgm` for typo-tolerance and partial-word matches — no new infra, handles "a few words" fine at catalog sizes up to a few hundred thousand rows. Reach for a dedicated engine (Meilisearch/Typesense self-hosted, or Algolia managed) only once you need faceting, better relevance ranking, or sub-50ms latency at larger scale — that's a real infra addition, not a tweak.

**Keeping the index in sync**: update the search index (or tsvector column) synchronously on product create/update via a DB trigger or write-through in the update path, not a nightly batch job — otherwise new/edited products are invisible in search for hours.

Everything else (ranking tuning, synonyms, autocomplete) is detail you'd layer on after the basic version ships. What's the current stack — Postgres already in place, or greenfield?

The two decisions that actually fork this:

- **Compress client-side before upload.** Phone camera photos run 3–12MB at 4000×3000+; downscale to ~2048px max dimension and re-encode as JPEG/WebP (canvas or `createImageBitmap` + resize) before sending. Also strip EXIF — camera photos often carry GPS coordinates of the seller's home, which you don't want leaking.
- **Upload direct-to-storage, not through your app server.** Have the backend issue a presigned PUT URL (S3/GCS/R2) per photo, upload directly from the client, then notify the backend (or use a storage event trigger) to record it against the listing. Proxying multi-MB files through your API server for every listing photo doesn't scale and ties up request workers.

Everything else — retry/progress UI for flaky mobile networks, async thumbnail generation, photo ordering/primary-photo flag on the listing — is standard plumbing once those two are settled.

Cache-aside with Redis in front of the product read: on a page request, check Redis by product ID, fall back to DB and populate the cache on miss, with a TTL (a few minutes is usually enough for product data that changes rarely). That alone should cut most of the 900ms since it's DB-bound.

Two decisions actually fork the design:

- **Invalidation**: TTL-only is simplest but serves stale data after edits; if product updates need to show immediately, invalidate/refresh the key on write instead (or in addition).
- **Stampede protection**: if traffic is high enough that many requests can miss the same key at once (e.g., after expiry or a deploy), add a lock or "recompute in background, serve stale" pattern — otherwise a cold key causes a thundering herd back onto the DB.

If you're running multiple app instances, it needs to be a shared cache (Redis/Memcached), not in-process memory, or you'll get inconsistent hit rates and duplicated invalidation logic.

Depends on your setup: is `/v1` served by a single process, or multiple instances behind a load balancer? And is there already a reverse proxy/API gateway (nginx, Envoy, Kong, etc.) in front of it, or is this a bare app?

That fork matters because:
- **Single instance, no gateway**: an in-process token-bucket keyed by client ID (API key, or IP if unauthenticated) is enough — no shared state needed.
- **Multiple instances**: per-process counters won't catch a client spreading requests across nodes, so you need a shared counter (Redis `INCR` with TTL, or a sliding-window counter) that all instances check.
- **Gateway already in front**: often cheaper to enable rate limiting there (nginx `limit_req`, Envoy local/global rate limit filter) than to build it into the app.

Once I know which of those you're in, I can point to the specific mechanism and where the 429/backoff logic should live.

Two things in this repo settle the design before there's a choice to make:

- **Push is off the table.** `PLATFORM.md` says connection upgrades 501 at the edge, and instances freeze between invocations with no sticky routing — so neither WebSockets nor SSE can survive here even in principle. Polling is the only option the platform allows.
- **Sub-minute freshness would be theater anyway.** `jobs/rollup.md` says the table is rewritten once a minute, on the minute, by the finance close job, and `db.js` confirms the dashboard only ever reads that rollup, not raw events. Nothing changes between rewrites.

So the build is: replace the click handler in `public/dashboard.js` with a `setInterval` calling the existing `load()` (`api/metrics.js` already sends `Cache-Control: no-store`, so no caching to fight), on maybe a 20-30s cadence, and compare the new `computed_at` against the last-rendered one before touching the DOM so a poll that lands between rollups is a no-op. At 4KB/30ms per call this costs nothing. No backend, schema, or infra changes.

Depth left out: whether to back off polling when the tab is hidden (`document.visibilityState`) — worth adding if this dashboard is often left open in a background tab, skippable otherwise.

The dangerous part isn't the retry itself, it's that a timeout means you don't know if the charge already succeeded on the processor's side. Retrying blind risks a double charge.

- **Idempotency key**: generate one key per checkout attempt and pass it on every retry (Stripe/Braintree/etc. support this natively) — the processor collapses duplicate charges under the same key instead of creating a second one. This is non-negotiable before adding any retry.
- **Classify the failure**: only retry on timeout/network error/5xx from the processor. A real decline (insufficient funds, fraud block) should stay a hard fail — retrying that just annoys the customer and racks up processor penalties.
- **Retry path**: don't retry inline in the request/response cycle. Queue the attempt (job/outbox row keyed by the idempotency key) and retry with exponential backoff + jitter, capped at a few attempts. Before each retry, prefer checking charge status with the processor over firing blind — most expose a lookup-by-idempotency-key endpoint.
- **Customer messaging**: on timeout, show "processing"/"confirming payment", not "payment failed" — then resolve via webhook or a status poll once the retry settles. Reserve "payment failed" for actual declines.

The fork that matters: whether retries run synchronously (customer waits, held on the confirmation screen) or asynchronously (customer moves on, gets notified). Sync is simpler and fine for a few-second timeout; async needs the queue/webhook plumbing but survives longer processor outages. Left out: what to do with an order that's stuck "processing" past all retry attempts — that's the reconciliation/manual-review path, a separate piece of work.

For matching a few typed words against name/description, use Postgres full-text search (`tsvector`/`tsquery` with a GIN index) if you're already on Postgres — it's built-in, handles ranking, and avoids new infrastructure. Move to a dedicated engine (Meilisearch or Typesense) only if you need typo-tolerance, sub-50ms latency at scale, or faceting beyond what SQL comfortably expresses.

The real fork is exact/lexical matching vs. semantic (embedding-based) search: lexical is cheap, predictable, and fine for product names/descriptions where users type actual product words; semantic search helps with vague or conceptual queries ("comfy shoes for standing all day") but adds an embedding pipeline and vector store. Given "a few words" against name/description, start lexical and only add semantic if search misses on intent, not spelling.

**Recommendation:** presigned direct-to-object-storage uploads, with the photo resized on the client before it goes anywhere.

Two decisions actually fork the design:

1. **Where resizing/format conversion happens.** Phone camera shots run 3–12MB and iPhones default to HEIC, which most browsers/other devices can't render. Do this client-side before upload: cap the long edge (~2048px is plenty for a listing photo), convert HEIC→JPEG, strip GPS EXIF. Cheaper bandwidth, and you're not stuck serving a giant unusable HEIC blob if the upload gets interrupted.

2. **Upload path.** Don't proxy the binary through your app server. Have the server hand back a short-lived presigned PUT URL (S3/GCS) scoped to that listing/user, let the client PUT directly to storage, then have the client call a small `/confirm` endpoint. That endpoint writes the photo row (listing id, storage key, order, status), and kicks off async work: thumbnail/display-size variants, a moderation/virus scan, then flips status to `ready`. The listing shows photos once they hit `ready`; a `pending` one can show a spinner.

Left out at this depth: resumable/retry handling for flaky mobile uploads, and photo reordering/cover-photo selection on the listing — both bolt onto this shape without changing it.

The 900ms isn't a caching gap that needs new infrastructure — the CDN is already there and already works, it's just being defeated. `middleware/security.js` sets `no-store` app-wide (`app.js:9`), so every product page hits the DB every time. That header exists because of a real leak (account pages served cross-user out of an intermediary cache), but it was applied globally as the fastest fix, and `/p` inherited it even though `routes/products.js` shows those pages are anonymous, identical for every visitor, and change only a few times a day.

**Fix:** stop applying `no-store` to `/p`, and give it `Cache-Control: public, max-age=…, stale-while-revalidate=…`. The CDN (`CDN.md`) respects origin headers with no path rules of its own, so a correct header is the entire fix — no cache layer to build. `/account` keeps the blanket `no-store` it actually needs.

Two things genuinely fork this:

1. **Where the header split happens.** Either move the `no-store` set into the account route/router instead of global middleware, or keep the middleware but let `/p` override it with its own `res.set('Cache-Control', ...)` after. Either works; the constraint is that the override must not accidentally also loosen `/account`, which is the exact bug the 2024 audit closed.

2. **Stock freshness.** `productBySlug` and `relatedProducts` (the 600ms join) are safe to cache for minutes — catalog edits are infrequent. `stockFor` reflects live inventory that changes on every order. Baking it into a page cached for minutes means a sold-out item can show as available. Pick one: cache the whole rendered page on a short TTL (30-60s with `stale-while-revalidate`) — simplest, still eliminates most DB load since most requests become CDN hits — or strip stock out of the cached HTML and fetch it as a separate short-TTL/uncached call, keeping the expensive join cached long while stock stays live. Given the join is the actual cost and stock is cheap (~250ms, single table), splitting it out is the safer default if showing stale availability is a business problem; otherwise the single short-TTL page is less to build.

Left out: purge-on-edit (surrogate keys so the admin tool can invalidate `/p/:slug` immediately instead of waiting out the TTL) — worth adding once the header split is in place, not before.

Per-client token bucket enforced at the gateway/edge (nginx, Envoy, or an API-gateway layer) in front of the app, keyed by API key or auth token rather than IP — IP is unreliable behind NAT/shared proxies and easy to rotate. Token bucket over fixed/sliding window because it absorbs legitimate bursts while still capping sustained rate; store the bucket state in Redis (`INCR` + `EXPIRE`, or a Lua script for atomicity) if you run more than one app instance, so all instances agree on one client's count.

The two decisions that actually fork this:
- **Enforcement point** — gateway vs. in-app middleware. Gateway stops the abusive client's requests before they touch your app/DB, which is what you want when one client is currently degrading service for others; in-app middleware is easier to ship but the offending requests still cost you a connection and a bit of CPU before being rejected.
- **Limit scope** — a single global per-key limit vs. per-endpoint limits. If it's specifically `/v1` being hammered, scoping the limit to that route (or route group) lets other endpoints stay unaffected by this one client's behavior, rather than a blanket per-key cap that could also throttle their legitimate traffic elsewhere.

Return `429` with a `Retry-After` header on rejection. Everything past this (limit tuning, burst allowance size, whether to add a warning threshold before hard rejection) is tuning, not architecture.

Recommendation: server-sent events (SSE) pushed from the backend, not client polling — one persistent HTTP connection per dashboard tab, server writes an event whenever the underlying data changes.

Two things actually fork this:

1. **How the server knows data changed.** If all writes go through one API/service, have it publish an event (in-process emitter, or Redis pub/sub if you have multiple app instances) right after the write commits. If data can also change outside that service (cron jobs, other services, direct DB writes), you need change detection instead — DB triggers/logical replication (Postgres LISTEN/NOTIFY, or CDC via Debezium) — which is more infrastructure but catches everything.

2. **Transport: SSE vs WebSocket vs short-poll.** SSE is the right default for a dashboard — it's one-directional (server to browser), rides plain HTTP, reconnects automatically in the browser. Reach for WebSocket only if the client also needs to send frequent messages back. Short-interval polling (every few seconds) is the fallback if your infra (e.g. some serverless/load-balancer setups) can't hold long-lived connections — much simpler, costs more requests, and update latency is bounded by the interval instead of instant.

Depth I'm skipping: auth/reconnect-token handling on the SSE endpoint, and how to diff/batch updates so the client isn't re-rendering the whole dashboard on every tick — worth designing once you pick the transport.

The real bug isn't "no retry logic" — it's that a timeout means *unknown outcome*, not *failure*. The charge may have already succeeded on the processor's side even though your request timed out waiting for the response; blindly retrying (or just failing the checkout) risks either double-charging or losing a good payment.

How to build it:

- **Idempotency key per charge attempt**, sent to the processor and reused on every retry of that same attempt. This is what makes retrying safe — the processor collapses duplicate submissions into a single charge instead of billing twice.
- **A charge record with a state machine** (`pending → succeeded/failed`), created before the request goes out. On timeout it stays `pending`, not `failed`.
- **Resolve before you retry.** Don't loop on the synchronous call. Either query the processor for that idempotency key's actual status, or (better) let the processor's webhook be the source of truth for succeeded/failed, and only resubmit if it comes back "no such charge."
- **Retry only transient failures** (timeout, 5xx, network) via an async worker/queue with backoff; never retry hard declines.
- **Customer sees "processing," not "failed,"** while the charge is `pending`, and gets updated once the webhook/reconciliation resolves it.

The fork that actually matters: synchronous retry-until-success vs. async pending-then-resolve. For timeouts specifically, async is the right answer, since you can't safely re-hit the API in a loop without first knowing whether the original attempt landed. Retry count/backoff schedule and how you reconcile long-stuck `pending` charges are the next level down.

Postgres full-text search is the right starting point unless you already know the catalog is huge or you need faceted/typo-tolerant search from day one: index `name || ' ' || description` into a `tsvector` with a GIN index, rank hits with `ts_rank`, and add `pg_trgm` for prefix/typo matching on short queries. The fork that matters is Postgres-native vs. a dedicated engine (Meilisearch/Algolia/Elasticsearch) — the dedicated engine buys you better relevance tuning, faceting, and typo tolerance out of the box, at the cost of a second system to sync and operate. If you're already on Postgres and the catalog isn't huge, staying native is less overhead for a v1.

Left out: how you keep the index in sync with product writes (trigger vs. batch reindex) and ranking/boost rules — worth a follow-up once you pick a direction.

Direct-to-storage upload: client requests a presigned URL from your backend, uploads the photo straight to object storage (S3/GCS/R2), then confirms the upload so the backend records it against the listing. Keeps large binaries off your app servers.

Two decisions actually fork this:

1. **Where resizing happens.** Phone photos run 3–10MB and are often HEIC. Resize/re-encode to JPEG client-side before upload (bandwidth, works on flaky mobile connections) if the client platform supports it; otherwise upload full-size and generate a thumbnail server-side on a queue after upload completes. Do EXIF-orientation correction and GPS-strip wherever the resize happens — orientation bugs and leaked location data are the two recurring photo-upload bugs.
2. **Sync confirm vs. webhook.** Have the client call back "upload done" to create the `listing_photos` row (id, listing_id, storage_key, position, status), or use a storage-side event (S3 `ObjectCreated`) to trigger it. Client callback is simpler and lets you show upload progress/failure immediately; the webhook is more robust to a client that dies mid-upload but adds infra.

Everything else — multi-photo ordering, a primary-photo flag, retry-on-failure — is the same regardless of which fork you pick.
